pitch: I build and own a production multi-agent LLM platform at Johnson & Johnson that serves biomedical scientists and drug-safety teams under FDA/EMA regulation. It's six agents — an orchestrator coordinating five specialists — running on Azure Kubernetes Service over 10,000-plus internal scientific documents. In production it cut research turnaround by 22%, reduced hallucination by roughly 18%, and sustains 120 concurrent sessions at p95 latency under 900 milliseconds. The hard part wasn't the model; it was making it grounded, auditable, and trustworthy enough to ship in a regulated pharma environment.

slides.label: The problem
slides.text: At Johnson & Johnson, a major challenge was that critical safety information was scattered across dozens of systems — clinical trials, adverse event reports, regulatory documents, and internal knowledge bases. When a potential safety signal appeared — an early warning that a drug or medical product might be causing an unexpected side effect or risk — analysts had to manually search through all of it to piece together the full picture. That process was slow, inconsistent, and risky, especially in an environment where missing a signal could impact patient safety and regulatory compliance.

slides.label: The solution
slides.text: The Generative AI platform was built to solve that. Instead of forcing teams to search in ten places, we created a single system that could retrieve, reason over, and summarize trusted internal evidence in seconds.

slides.label: An example
slides.text: For example, if a pharmacovigilance analyst suspects a drug might be linked to liver toxicity, they can ask the system a direct question. Behind the scenes, the platform retrieves relevant clinical trial data, adverse event cases, and regulatory history, filters it by drug and condition, and feeds only that verified evidence into the language model. The response they get is not a guess — it is a grounded, traceable summary of what J&J already knows, with citations to the original sources.

slides.label: My role
slides.text: As the lead engineer, I was responsible for making sure this entire flow worked end-to-end: ingestion of sensitive documents, secure and compliant retrieval, hybrid search accuracy, and safe generation of answers. I worked with safety scientists, regulatory teams, and cloud engineers to ensure the system was not only technically sound, but trustworthy enough to support real safety decisions.

slides.label: The result
slides.text: The result was a dramatic reduction in time spent searching for information, fewer duplicated analyses, and faster, more confident safety and regulatory decisions. We effectively turned J&J’s fragmented knowledge into a single, reliable source of truth that teams could query in real time — which is exactly what modern enterprise AI is supposed to do.

jj.sub: RAGAS and the seven layers · J&J multi-agent platform
jj.title: Seven views that must agree
jj.thesis: Open scientific Q&A has no single right answer, so no single score decides a release on the J&J platform. Seven layers each measure one thing. RAGAS scores two of them; the other five exist because RAGAS cannot see trajectories, hard compliance rules, production behaviour or expert judgment.

layers.name: Retrieval
layers.lead: Context precision and context recall — measured separately from what the model did with the evidence.
layers.body: Run on every index or chunking change. If only the final answer were measured, a retrieval regression would look like a generation problem and get tuned in the wrong place.

layers.name: Generation
layers.q: Is the answer supported by its context?
layers.lead: Faithfulness to the supplied context, scored by an LLM judge that is itself validated against human labels.
layers.body: Regression-gated in CI with a threshold fixed before the change. A faithfulness score is only as trustworthy as the judge behind it, which is why layer 7 checks the judge.

layers.name: Agent trajectory
layers.q: Did the orchestrator plan and delegate sensibly?
layers.lead: Whether the orchestrator called the right specialists, with the right tasks, in a sensible order.
layers.body: Retrieval and generation can both look healthy while the plan is wrong — Drug Safety never called on a pharmacovigilance question, for example. Trajectories are read from the traces.

layers.name: Task success
layers.q: Did the user get what they needed?
layers.lead: Scored on realistic workflows, not on isolated question-answer pairs.
layers.body: Component metrics can all pass while the product still fails the user. This is the layer closest to the outcome scientists care about.

layers.name: Safety & compliance
layers.q: Does every citation resolve to its evidence?
layers.lead: Citation integrity — a hard gate, pass or fail.
layers.body: Checked in code, not by a judge: citation IDs not in the run’s evidence store are stripped at each specialist and again at the orchestrator. No faithfulness score can buy back a failure here.

layers.name: Operational
layers.q: What happens once real users touch it?
layers.lead: Production behaviour: refusal rate, citation coverage, retrieval hit rate and query drift.
layers.body: Quality signals move before CPU notices. Refusal rate is watched in both directions — a sudden drop usually means a gate broke, not that quality improved. Queries drift faster than the corpus.

layers.name: SME review
layers.lead: Expert judgment on a sampled set, on a recurring cadence.
layers.body: Automated evaluation scales; SME review keeps it honest. Findings feed back into the labeled eval sets, and the same labels are what the LLM judge is validated against.

steps: Start from the experts
The POC began with an SME question set with document-backed answers, scored blind side by side against the base model.
Reference answer plus evidence
Each question carries a reference answer and the documents that support it — context recall and precision cannot be scored without them.
Held out
Release candidates are scored on held-out Q&A, so a change is judged on questions it was not tuned against.
Agent fixtures beside it
Knowledge adds closure-table fixtures (a parent concept must return its whole subtree); Drug Safety adds seriousness-criteria cases with MedDRA coding and E2B(R3) structure.
Synthetic expansion

RAGAS can generate questions from the corpus: it builds a knowledge graph over the documents, then synthesizes single-hop specific (50%), multi-hop abstract (25%) and multi-hop specific (25%) queries, each with a reference answer. Synthetic questions widen coverage, but enter the golden set only after SME review.
Versioned and controlled
Eval datasets are validated artifacts under change control. SME findings are added as new reviewed versions, never edited in place.
golden.note: Every validation summary names the eval dataset version it used, so a test set can never change silently under a release.

detail.say: Six services on one cluster, released independently.

iv.short: The runtime is one AKS cluster running six services: the orchestrator and five specialists — Knowledge, Ontology, Drug Safety, QA and Summarization. It’s one container image with a SERVICE build argument, six Deployments, shipped as a Helm chart. Each service has its own pipeline and release cadence, every pod has its own Workload Identity, and KEDA scales each specialist on its own Service Bus subscription.

qa.q: Why one cluster instead of a cluster per agent?
qa.a: Six services on one cluster gives us isolation at the deployment level without six sets of platform overhead. Each service is its own Deployment with its own identity and its own pipeline, so a Drug Safety change never waits on a Summarization release — and never risks one either.

qa.q: Why six services instead of one application?
qa.a: The agents change at different speeds and carry different risk. Drug Safety needs a pharmacovigilance SME to approve and a 2% first canary ring; Summarization doesn’t. As separate deployables, each one gets the release process its risk deserves.

Each specialist scales with KEDA on the message count of its own subscription — one ScaledObject for stable, one for canary. The orchestrator scales on CPU with HPA. Under load test we sustained 120 concurrent sessions.

qa.q: How do you ship a new version of one agent?

detail.head: Two indexes, one query pattern, every filter applied before a chunk is retrieved.
detail.role: The retrieval surface: two indexes, one query pattern.
how: Dense plus BM25, fused by reciprocal rank, then reranked
Every chunk carries entity and ancestor IDs, tier and effective date
Filters are applied in the query, never after retrieval
detail.dh: Filters in the query beat filtering the result set.
detail.dec: Post-filtering means the model may have already seen text the caller was not entitled to. Putting tier, effective date and ancestor IDs into the search query itself is what makes retrieval an access-control boundary rather than a convenience.
detail.say: Ingestion prepares the evidence, terminology normalizes it, and AI Search retrieves it with filters in the query.

iv.short: Retrieval is Azure AI Search with one query pattern everywhere: dense vectors plus BM25, fused by reciprocal rank, then reranked. There are two indexes — kb-knowledge for the general scientific corpus and kb-compliance for governed content. The rule that matters: tier, effective date and ancestor IDs go into the query itself, never onto the result set, so retrieval is an access-control boundary.

qa.q: Why hybrid search instead of pure vector search?
qa.a: Scientific text is full of exact identifiers — drug names, MedDRA terms, study codes — that keyword search catches and embeddings blur. Dense retrieval catches paraphrase. Reciprocal rank fusion combines the two lists without calibrating their scores, and the reranker orders the final set.

qa.q: Why filter in the query rather than after retrieval?
qa.a: If you post-filter, the model may already have seen text the caller wasn’t entitled to. Putting tier, effective date and ancestor IDs into the search query makes retrieval itself the access-control boundary, not a convenience.

qa.q: Why two indexes instead of one with a security flag?
qa.a: Separation at the infrastructure level is a compliance story an auditor can verify; a flag in application code is not. The governed index is readable only by the Drug Safety identity, because its Search role is scoped to that index.

qa.q: How do you know retrieval is good?
qa.a: It’s the first layer of our seven-layer eval: RAGAS context precision and recall, measured separately from what the model did with the evidence, on every index or chunking change. Knowledge also has closure-table fixtures — a parent-concept query must return the whole subtree.

push.q: What happens when retrieval comes back thin?
push.a: The system is allowed to say the context doesn’t contain the answer. A specialist never returns an uncited “answered” — it’s downgraded to insufficient_evidence — and refusal under thin retrieval is part of the red-team suite in every release.

detail.dec: A graph answers richer questions than we ever ask on the hot path. What retrieval needs is the ancestor set, which is knowable at ingestion. Building it as an artifact removed a whole tier of infrastructure and a place for a generated query to go wrong.
detail.say: The terminology layer is built during ingestion so AI Search can filter by concepts instead of traversing a graph at query time.

iv.short: Scientists ask about a parent concept and expect the child terms too. Instead of a graph database at query time, we ship the ontology as two versioned artifacts: a term dictionary that maps synonyms to a canonical entity ID, and a closure table of every concept’s ancestors. qa.a: A graph answers richer questions than we ever ask on the hot path. What retrieval needs is the ancestor set, and that’s knowable at ingestion. Building it as an artifact removed a whole tier of infrastructure and a place for a generated query to go wrong — for roughly ninety percent of the value.

qa.q: Which vocabularies, and how are terms resolved?
qa.a: MedDRA, SNOMED CT and MeSH form the terminology spine. The dictionary maps synonyms and abbreviations to one canonical ID, and a lookup is exact or found:false — no nearest-neighbour guesses.

qa.q: How do you keep the index in step with vocabulary updates?
qa.a: Each vocabulary release rebuilds both artifacts and triggers a re-stamp of the affected chunks. So the index and the closure table are always the same version.

qa.q: When would you use a graph?
qa.a: For discovering novel links between entities across the literature. That’s a different product. For filtering retrieval by concept, a precomputed closure is simpler and deterministic.

detail.dec: Nothing in this layer runs at query time. A Blob event opens one idempotent job, so re-running a batch is safe and a document is never embedded twice at the same version.
detail.say: Ingestion and ETL turn source documents into versioned, searchable evidence for the AKS services.

iv.short: Ingestion is the batch path — nothing in it runs at query time. A Blob event opens one idempotent job per document: Document Intelligence parses layout and tables, Databricks chunks by structure, entity stamping writes entity IDs and all ancestors onto each chunk, and text-embedding-3-large vectorizes it. A document is embedded exactly once per version, and everything can be rebuilt from the immutable original.

qa.q: Why event-driven batch instead of indexing on demand?
qa.a: Because re-running has to be safe. One idempotent job per document per version means a retry never double-embeds, and nothing on the request path waits for parsing.

qa.q: How do you handle updates and re-embedding?
qa.a: Index writes are incremental upserts and staleness is monitored, because a stale index gives confident, outdated answers. Re-embedding is a versioned, replayable pipeline run, and the embedding model version is recorded on every chunk.

push.q: Is anything in ingestion on the request path?

qa.q: How did the users shape the design?

qa.q: Why Front Door in front of API Management?
qa.a: Front Door handles the edge — TLS, WAF and routing. APIM handles policy — who the caller is and what they may do. Keeping them separate keeps the cluster and the agents private while the platform still gets a resilient, globally managed entry point.

qa.q: Why not expose the AKS ingress directly?
qa.a: A managed edge beats putting an in-cluster ingress on the internet. AKS and the agents stay off the public internet entirely; only validated traffic continues to APIM.

qa.q: Does the WAF handle prompt injection?

push.a: Each layer has one job — edge, policy, cluster entry — and the end-to-end p95 still stays under 900 milliseconds. The layers are what let the agents assume every request is already authenticated, authorized and traced.

qa.q: Why put policy in APIM instead of the application?
qa.a: So the agents never make access decisions. Quotas, rate limits and correlation IDs live at the gateway; when a consumer needs a different limit, nothing in the platform changes.

qa.q: What is the correlation ID used for?
qa.a: It’s the spine of the audit trail. It’s stamped at APIM, carried as a Service Bus message property through every agent hop, used for fan-in on the reply queue, and it keys the Cosmos record. Every claim resolves by correlation ID to its chunks, versions, model deployment and verifier verdict.

qa.q: How do you protect the platform from a noisy consumer?
qa.a: Per-consumer quotas and rate limits at APIM, off the orchestrator’s hot path. Downstream, each specialist scales on its own subscription, so one heavy workload doesn’t starve the others.

push.q: Why not handle auth and quotas inside the FastAPI service?

qa.q: How do the specialists get work, then?

The orchestrator’s FastAPI /chat endpoint, running the OpenAI Agents SDK. From there, everything is internal.

detail.say: The orchestrator reasons; it doesn’t just route. It has one tool, because delegation is the only thing it decides.

iv.short: The orchestrator is the reasoning core. It runs gpt-5.4 on the OpenAI Agents SDK behind a FastAPI endpoint, plans the request, decides which specialists to call and what runs in parallel, then assembles the cited answer. qa.q: Why let the model plan instead of a fixed workflow graph?
qa.a: A framework graph where every hop is an explicit node makes control flow legible but freezes it — every new question shape needs a new branch. Letting the model plan keeps the platform open-ended. The governance sits in the gates around the model, not in a hardcoded graph.

A tool should exist only where the model makes a real decision. Loading the session, validating, saving and tracing used to be tools, and the model could skip one — or validate draft A and return draft B. Now they run as code on every request, and the model’s only choice is who to delegate to.

It’s an RPC over Service Bus. It publishes to the agent’s topic with a correlation ID and a track property, then parks an asyncio Future; a reply listener in the same pod resolves it. Parallel tool calls give fan-out, and the correlation ID gives fan-in.

qa.q: How do you handle failures and timeouts?
qa.a: The orchestrator owns retries and timeouts; agents never retry each other. Deadlines nest — the specialist budget inside the invoke_agent wait inside the HTTP budget — so a slow agent degrades the answer instead of hanging the request.

qa.a: They used to be LLM tools. As tools, the model could skip one, or validate draft A and return draft B. As code they run on every request and can’t be skipped. The rule I use: a tool exists only where the model makes a real decision.

The model’s plan and decision notes, the session context that was injected, and what the code observed — written to Cosmos by correlation ID and to OpenTelemetry. That lets us reconstruct any answer months later without Redis.

detail.hard: When parallelism was needed, the answer was for the orchestrator to publish a partial request as soon as the knowledge leg landed — not to let QA self-trigger off an event it wasn’t addressed on.

iv.short: Between the orchestrator and the five specialists sits Azure Service Bus, with one topic per agent. qa.q: Why a topic per agent instead of one shared topic?
qa.a: With one shared topic, an agent could pick up work addressed to another. In this domain that means validating the wrong artifact, retrying work nobody owns, and a broken audit trail. A topic per agent keeps that isolation and still allows an exact canary split.

qa.q: How does the canary split work?
qa.a: The orchestrator stamps track on every request at the rollout’s current weight, hashing the session ID so one conversation stays on one version. Stable pods read the stable subscription, canary pods the canary one. Outside a rollout the weight is zero.

qa.q: How does a reply find the right orchestrator pod?
qa.a: orchestrator-replies is session-enabled, and the session ID is the orchestrator pod’s name. Each reply lands on the replica holding the waiting Future, and fan-in is by correlation ID.

qa.q: Why Service Bus rather than Kafka or Event Hubs?
qa.a: We needed per-message features more than stream throughput: sessions to route a reply to a pod, subscription filters for the canary split, dead-lettering, and Entra RBAC per entity. Those are native to Service Bus; with Kafka we’d have built them ourselves.

push.q: Why not approximate the canary with a replica ratio?
push.a: A replica ratio only approximates the split. Drug Safety’s first ring is 2% with an SME pause, and you can’t hit 2% reliably with a handful of pods. Topic subscriptions give an exact split per request.

detail.head: The verifier: it reads the draft against the evidence and tries to break it. It is not a RAG consumer.

detail.hard: People read "QA agent" as a test-automation agent. It is a verifier: it sees the draft and the evidence, and its job is to disagree.
detail.say: The QA agent doesn’t retrieve anything. It reads the draft against the evidence and tries to break it.

iv.short: QA is quality assurance in the reasoning sense, not test automation. It’s an independent verifier on gpt-5.4 at high reasoning: it gets the draft and the evidence, checks that every claim is grounded, runs an n-sample consistency check, and returns pass or flag with a reason. It does no retrieval of its own, so it can’t be fooled by a fresh search.

qa.q: Why not let the generating agent check itself?
qa.a: A model grading its own output is not a control. QA sees the draft plus the retrieved spans and runs claim-grounding and self-consistency checks independently of the agent that wrote it.

If it could search, it could find new text that happens to support a claim the draft made without evidence. Verifying only against the evidence it’s handed means a claim is grounded in what was actually used, or it fails.

qa.q: What does the consistency check do?
qa.a: run_consistency_check samples several answers and measures their agreement. Low agreement is a signal that the evidence is thin or the question is ambiguous.
QA alone is about a third of a typical query’s cost, because reasoning tokens bill at the output rate. In pharmacovigilance, that’s the price of not shipping a confident wrong answer.

push.q: People hear “QA agent” and think tests. What is it really?
push.a: A verifier. It sees the draft and the evidence, and its job is to disagree.

detail.dh: Being slow and right beat being fast — high reasoning effort is the point.
detail.dec: False negatives are the asymmetric risk. The agent runs at high reasoning effort and is evaluated on seriousness-criteria recall, not overall accuracy.
detail.hard: False negatives are the asymmetric risk. The eval set for this agent is tuned against recall on seriousness criteria, not against overall accuracy.
detail.say: This agent is allowed to be the slowest one on the platform.

iv.short: Drug Safety is the regulated leg. Anything touching pharmacovigilance, labeling or submissions goes through it, and it queries only the governed kb-compliance index. It runs gpt-5.4 at high reasoning because here slow and right beats fast: seriousness criteria and MedDRA coding are checked, not inferred, against E2B(R3) structure.

qa.a: On seriousness-criteria recall, tuned against false negatives — not on overall accuracy — because a missed serious case is the asymmetric risk. The pipeline adds fixture gates for MedDRA coding and E2B(R3) structure.

qa.q: How is it isolated from the general knowledge base?
qa.a: Its identity has Search Index Data Reader on kb-compliance only, and the Knowledge identity can’t read kb-compliance at all. The separation is enforced by identity, not by a code path.

qa.q: How do you release a change to it?
qa.a: It’s the most conservative release on the platform. A pharmacovigilance SME is the required approver, the canary goes 2, 10, 50, 100 percent with an SME pause before the last step, and the release carries a Part 11 electronic signature.

qa.q: Why spend high reasoning effort here?
qa.a: Because being slow and right beats being fast. It’s the most expensive hop — about five cents of the eighteen-cent fan-out — and this is exactly where that spend belongs.

push.q: What if the evidence is incomplete?
push.a: It doesn’t infer. An uncited answer is downgraded to insufficient_evidence, and refusal is a valid, measured output. In pharmacovigilance, “the context does not contain this” beats a plausible guess.

detail.head: Resolves the question into the controlled vocabulary the corpus is indexed under.
how: Maps free text to MedDRA, SNOMED CT and MeSH concepts
Returns entity IDs plus ancestors so the Knowledge agent can filter on the whole subtree
Runs on a smaller model — this is lookup and normalization, not reasoning
detail.dh: A closure-table lookup beat a live graph traversal.
detail.dec: A runtime graph database would answer richer questions about how concepts relate. It was rejected for this workload: the ancestor set is what the retrieval actually needs, it is knowable at ingestion, and a traversal in the hot path adds infrastructure plus a place for the query itself to go wrong.
detail.say: Ontology is a lookup against a precomputed closure table, not a live graph traversal.

iv.short: The Ontology agent translates the question into the controlled vocabulary the corpus is indexed under. It maps free text to MedDRA, SNOMED CT and MeSH concepts and returns entity IDs plus ancestors, so Knowledge can filter on the whole subtree. It’s lookup and normalization, not reasoning, so it runs on gpt-5.4-mini.

qa.q: Why a separate agent for terminology?
qa.a: Because terminology has to be exact, and that’s easiest to guarantee in one narrow agent: lookups are exact or found:false, enforced in code, and the agent rejects any concept ID that wasn’t resolved in the same run.

qa.q: Why not a live graph traversal?
qa.a: A graph would answer richer questions about how concepts relate, but retrieval only needs the ancestor set, and that’s knowable at ingestion. A traversal on the hot path adds infrastructure plus a place for the query itself to go wrong.

qa.q: What happens with a term it doesn’t know?
qa.a: It says so. A fuzzy match on terminology is a hallucination with extra steps, so an unknown term returns not found, and the answer reflects that.

push.q: Isn’t exact match too brittle for how scientists type?
push.a: That’s what the dictionary is for: synonyms and abbreviations map to one canonical ID. And brittle is the safer failure — “not found” is visible, a wrong concept is silent.

detail.head: Answers the substantive scientific question against the internal corpus with hybrid retrieval.
how: Search-then-generate: one retrieval tool, one generation tool
Hybrid query — vector plus keyword — with entitlement and domain filters applied at the index
Concept expansion by closure-table filter rather than graph traversal
detail.dh: Search-then-generate with two tools beat an agent that improvises its own data access.
detail.dec: Every specialist has exactly one retrieval tool and one generation tool. Constraining the shape is what makes the trajectory evaluable and the audit trail complete.
detail.say: Every specialist is the same shape: search, then generate. Nothing improvises its own data access.

iv.short: Knowledge answers the substantive scientific question against the internal corpus. It’s search-then-generate with exactly two tools: search_enterprise_kb runs hybrid retrieval on kb-knowledge with the closure-table ancestor filter, and synthesize_knowledge writes the cited answer on gpt-5.4. Every specialist has that same shape — nothing improvises its own data access.

qa.q: Why constrain every agent to two tools?
qa.a: Constraining the shape is what makes the trajectory evaluable and the audit trail complete. If an agent could improvise its data access, we couldn’t say afterwards what it saw or why.

Ontology returns entity IDs plus ancestors; Knowledge filters on ancestor_ids, so a question about a parent concept retrieves chunks about every child term. It’s a filter in the query, not a graph traversal.

qa.q: How do you test it before release?
qa.a: Closure-table fixtures in the pipeline — a parent-concept query must return the whole subtree — plus the golden-set eval and the grounding gate, then a canary at 5, 20, 50 and 100 percent.
It cites per claim and may answer “the context does not contain this.” An uncited “answered” is downgraded to insufficient_evidence before it ever reaches the orchestrator.

push.q: How did you fix chunk granularity?
push.a: Big chunks buried the citations and small ones lost the meaning. Structural chunking with an overlap window tuned so a citation never straddles a chunk edge, plus hybrid retrieval and metadata filters, fixed it.

detail.head: The model deployments, called directly and synchronously by each agent — never through the bus.
how: Direct REST from agent to model — Service Bus sits between the orchestrator and the agents, never between an agent and the model
Model versions are pinned per agent so a platform-side model change is a change-controlled event
Prompt caching on the stable prefixes; batch pricing for ingestion-time work
detail.dh: Direct REST from agent to model beat routing model calls through the bus.
detail.dec: Service Bus decouples orchestration from agents. Putting it in front of the model would add latency and a queue to a call that is inherently synchronous, with nothing gained.
detail.hard: When GPT-4o was retired the migration had to be per-agent, with the eval suite rerun for each. A model swap in a validated system is a release, not a config change.
detail.say: The bus decouples orchestration from agents. It does not sit in front of the model.

iv.short: The model deployments live in Azure OpenAI: the gpt-5.4 family for the agents and text-embedding-3-large for vectors. Each agent calls its own pinned deployment directly over synchronous REST with its own Workload Identity token. Service Bus decouples the orchestrator from the agents; it never sits in front of the model.

qa.q: Why not route model calls through the bus too?
qa.a: A model call is inherently synchronous. A queue in front of it adds latency and another moving part, with nothing gained.

qa.q: How do you manage model versions?
qa.a: Deployments are pinned per agent with auto-upgrade disabled, so a platform-side model change is a change-controlled event, not a surprise.

qa.q: Tell me about a model migration.
qa.a: We launched on GPT-4o. When it was retired, the migration had to be per agent, with the eval suite rerun for each. In a validated system, a model swap is a release, not a config change.

qa.q: How do you control model cost?
qa.a: Right-size per agent: gpt-5.4-mini for Ontology and Summarization, high reasoning only for Drug Safety and QA. Prompt caching on stable prefixes — cached input bills at about 10% of the input rate — and batch pricing for ingestion embeddings.

push.q: How do you know which agent drives cost?
push.a: Per-agent OpenTelemetry spans record p50 and p95 tokens per agent, and those feed the cost model. Drug Safety and QA are about 51% of a worst-case query, so that’s where any optimization starts.

detail.head: The session store and retrieval cache — working memory outside any pod.
how: Session context is loaded before each run and saved after validation, with a TTL
Retrieval cache keyed by query plus tier, so a cached result never crosses an entitlement boundary
A missing key means a turn without history, not a failed request; runs on the high-availability tier
detail.dh: Redis for working memory and Cosmos for the record beat one store doing both.
detail.dec: Session context is read before each run and written after validation, with a TTL. Because keys expire, the context injected into each run is also written to Cosmos with the trace. A missing key degrades to a turn without history rather than an error.
detail.hard: Redis is not the record. Keys expire and get evicted, so the session context injected into each run is also written to Cosmos with the trace. An answer can be reconstructed months later without Redis.
detail.say: Redis is working memory. Cosmos is the record.

iv.short: Azure Managed Redis is working memory outside any pod: the session store and the retrieval cache. Session context is loaded before each run and saved after validation, with a TTL. The cache key is query plus tier, so a cached result never crosses an entitlement boundary. Redis is working memory; Cosmos is the record.

qa.q: Why Redis for sessions instead of Cosmos?
qa.a: Session state is read and written on every turn and it’s disposable — that’s a fast, TTL’d store. Cosmos is the system of record. Keeping them separate means neither has to be good at the other’s job.

qa.q: What happens if a key is evicted?
qa.a: A missing key means a turn without history, not a failed request. And because the injected session context is also written to Cosmos with the trace, any answer can be reconstructed months later without Redis.

qa.q: How do you stop the cache leaking data across users?
qa.a: The cache key includes the caller’s tier, so a result cached for one entitlement level is never served to another. Fan-out queries aren’t cached at all — they rarely repeat, and they include the regulated Drug Safety hop.

qa.q: What happens to a session if a pod restarts?
qa.a: The session survives because it lives in Redis, not in the pod. An in-flight request doesn’t move pods, because its reply is routed to the pod holding the Future.

push.q: Isn’t caching regulated answers risky?
push.a: Yes, which is why it’s limited: TTLs or ingestion-triggered invalidation for regulated answers, no caching on fan-out queries, and regulators likely expect fresh, traceable validation on the Drug Safety and QA hops.

detail.head: The general scientific corpus, every chunk stamped with entity IDs, ancestor IDs, domain and security level.
detail.role: The general scientific corpus — 10,000+ documents across the eight-domain pharma taxonomy.

Every chunk carries entity IDs, ancestor IDs, domain tags and a security level
Entitlement filters are applied in the query, before anything is retrieved
detail.dh: One hybrid index with rich metadata beat many small topic indexes.
detail.say: Two indexes, not one. General knowledge and governed content never share a retrieval surface.

iv.short: kb-knowledge is the general scientific index: 10,000-plus documents across the eight-domain pharma taxonomy. Every chunk carries entity IDs, ancestor IDs, domain tags and a security level, and the query applies tier, effective date and ancestor filters before anything is retrieved. One hybrid index with rich metadata, not many small topic indexes.

qa.q: Why one big index instead of an index per topic?
qa.a: Metadata does the partitioning. With entity, ancestor, domain and security fields on every chunk, one hybrid index can be filtered to any slice, without routing questions between dozens of small indexes.
id, title, content, content_vector, uri, concept_ids, ancestor_ids and region, with a semantic configuration named default. The vector and the analyzed text live in the same document.
Only the Knowledge agent’s identity, through Search Index Data Reader scoped to kb-knowledge. And that identity can’t query kb-compliance at all.

qa.q: How do you keep it fresh?
qa.a: Incremental upserts from the ingestion job, with staleness monitored — a stale index gives confident, outdated answers. A vocabulary release re-stamps affected chunks, so the ancestors always match the closure table.

push.q: How do you evaluate retrieval separately from generation?
push.a: RAGAS context precision and recall on every index or chunking change — layer one of the eval program, measured apart from what the model did with the evidence.

detail.head: The governed index: SOPs, labels, submissions and safety records under change control, effective-dated and tiered.
how: Only the Drug Safety & Compliance agent can query it — its Search role is scoped to this index alone
Every document version is pinned; superseded versions stay retrievable for audit
Change control on the index is treated as change control on a validated system
detail.dh: A separate governed index beat a security flag on the shared one.
detail.dec: Governed content has its own index and its own agent. Separation at the infrastructure level is a compliance story an auditor can verify; a flag in application code is not.
stack: Drug Safety identity only, index-scoped role
detail.say: Governed content lives behind its own index and its own agent. That separation is the compliance story.

iv.short: kb-compliance is the governed index: SOPs, labels, submissions and safety records under change control. It’s effective-dated and tiered, every document version is pinned, and superseded versions stay retrievable for audit. Only the Drug Safety identity can read it — its Search role is scoped to this index alone. That separation is the compliance story.

qa.q: Why a separate index instead of a security flag?
qa.a: Separation at the infrastructure level is something an auditor can verify. A flag in application code is a promise; a role scoped to an index is a fact.
Because the audit question is what the system knew on a given date. Effective dating lets a query ask for the version in force, and retaining old versions lets us reproduce an earlier answer.

qa.q: How are changes to this index controlled?
qa.a: Change control on the index is treated as change control on a validated system: under 21 CFR Part 11 and GxP, every index change is a controlled change with an approval record.

push.q: What if Knowledge needs governed content to answer?
push.a: It doesn’t get it. Anything regulated is answered only by Drug Safety against the governed index, and the orchestrator assembles both legs. The Knowledge identity simply can’t read kb-compliance.

detail.head: The lookup that turns what a scientist typed into a canonical entity ID.
how: Synonyms and abbreviations resolve to one ID against the terminology spine (MedDRA, SNOMED CT, MeSH)
Exact match or found:false — there is no nearest-neighbour guess on a terminology lookup
Built by the Ontology Loader; versioned per vocabulary release
detail.dh: Exact match or found:false beat nearest-neighbour matching.
detail.hard: A fuzzy match on terminology is a hallucination with extra steps. If the term is not in the dictionary the answer is "not found", and the agent says so.
detail.say: Terminology lookup is exact or it fails loudly. We never guess a concept.

iv.short: The term dictionary turns what a scientist typed into a canonical entity ID. Synonyms and abbreviations resolve against the MedDRA, SNOMED CT and MeSH spine, and the rule is exact match or found:false — never a nearest-neighbour guess. It’s built by the Ontology Loader and versioned per vocabulary release.

qa.q: Why not fuzzy or embedding-based matching?
qa.a: A fuzzy match on terminology is a hallucination with extra steps. If the term isn’t in the dictionary, the answer is “not found,” and the agent says so.
In a Cosmos terminology container with label_normalized, synonyms_normalized, vocabulary, level and ancestor_ids. The Ontology agent has read-only access to it.

qa.q: How is the exact-match rule enforced?
qa.a: In code, not in the prompt. No nearest-neighbour candidates are ever shown to the model, and any concept ID not resolved in the same run is rejected.

push.q: What about misspellings?
push.a: Labels and synonyms are stored normalized, so case and spacing don’t matter, but a genuine misspelling returns not found. That’s deliberate: a visible miss is safer than a silent wrong concept.

nodes.name: Closure table
nodes.sub: entity → all ancestors · versioned per release

detail.head: The ontology flattened at ingestion, so retrieval never has to traverse anything.
how: Each chunk is stamped with its own entity IDs plus every parent and ancestor ID
A parent-concept question becomes an index filter across the whole subtree
Rebuilt as a batch artifact when the terminology spine updates
detail.dh: Option B, metadata filtering, beat Option A, a runtime graph database.
detail.dec: Option A was Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin with runtime traversal. Option B — this one — gets roughly ninety percent of the value at a fraction of the infrastructure, with zero hallucination risk on the retrieval query itself. A graph is the right tool for discovering novel links between disparate literature entities; that is a different product.
detail.hard: The pushback was that GraphRAG over-complicates the design, and it was right. The honest version of this story is that the simpler design won on the merits.
detail.say: We precompute the ancestor closure at ingestion, so concept expansion is a filter, not a traversal.

iv.short: The closure table is the ontology flattened at ingestion. For every concept it stores all of its ancestors, and each chunk is stamped with its own entity IDs plus every parent and ancestor. So a question about a parent concept becomes an index filter across the whole subtree — retrieval never traverses anything.

qa.q: Walk me through the options you considered.
qa.a: Option A was Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin with runtime traversal. Option B, this one, precomputes the ancestor closure and filters on it. B gets roughly ninety percent of the value at a fraction of the infrastructure, with zero hallucination risk on the retrieval query itself.

qa.q: When would a graph be the right tool?
qa.a: For discovering novel links between entities across the literature. That’s a different product from filtering retrieval by concept.
Closure-table fixtures gate every Knowledge release: a parent-concept query must return the whole subtree.
It’s rebuilt as a batch artifact when the terminology spine updates, versioned per vocabulary release, and each release triggers a re-stamp of the affected chunks.

push.q: What does “zero hallucination risk on the query” mean?
push.a: With a graph, a generated query decides what to traverse, and a wrong query silently returns the wrong subtree. With a precomputed filter, the query is a list of IDs that came from an exact lookup — there’s nothing for a model to make up.

how: CSRs, safety labels, submissions, ELN entries, literature, patents
Immutable originals; everything downstream is derived and rebuildable

detail.dec: The raw document is never what we retrieve — it is what we can always go back to. Every downstream artifact is derived and rebuildable from it.
detail.say: The raw document is never the thing we retrieve. It’s the thing we can always go back to.

iv.short: Blob Storage is the landing zone for source documents across the eight pharma domains — clinical study reports, safety labels, submissions, ELN entries, literature and patents. The originals are immutable. An Event Grid event starts one ingestion job per document, and everything downstream is derived and can be rebuilt from the original.

qa.a: The raw document is never what we retrieve — it’s what we can always go back to. If parsing, chunking or the embedding model changes, we rebuild from source instead of patching derived data.
Each new or changed document emits a discrete event that opens one idempotent job, so re-running is safe and a document is embedded exactly once per version.

qa.q: Who reads the raw documents at request time?
qa.a: Only Summarization, with Storage Blob Data Reader, for fetch_and_chunk_doc. Every other agent works from the indexes.

push.q: How do you handle a corrected document?
push.a: A new version lands as a new immutable original and opens a new job, embedded once at that version. For governed content, the superseded version stays retrievable for audit.

detail.head: Turns scientific PDFs into structure instead of a wall of text.

Table structure survives as structure, which is what makes safety tables usable
detail.dh: Layout-aware parsing beat naive PDF text extraction.
detail.hard: Naive PDF extraction scrambled multi-column CSR pages into unusable chunks. This was the single biggest quality jump in the whole ingestion path.
detail.say: Parsing was a bigger lever on answer quality than any model change we made.

iv.short: Document Intelligence turns scientific PDFs into structure instead of a wall of text. We run v4.0 with the 2024-11-30 layout model, which keeps multi-column layout, tables and figure captions intact, with an OCR gate for scanned pages. Parsing was a bigger lever on answer quality than any model change we made.

qa.a: Naive PDF extraction scrambled multi-column CSR pages into unusable chunks. Layout-aware parsing was the single biggest quality jump in the whole ingestion path.

qa.q: Why do tables matter so much?
qa.a: Safety data lives in tables. Flatten a table into text and you lose which value belongs to which row and column. Keeping table structure is what makes safety tables usable for retrieval and citation.
An OCR gate handles scanned pages, so they enter the same structured path as born-digital PDFs.

push.q: Why not an open-source PDF parser?
push.a: We needed layout, tables and captions preserved on multi-column regulatory documents, inside the Azure boundary, with a pinned model version for change control. Document Intelligence gave us that as a managed, versioned service.

detail.head: Structural chunking and metadata tagging as a batch job — domain, tier, date, type on every chunk.

how: Respects section boundaries rather than character counts
Overlap tuned so a citation never straddles a chunk edge
detail.dh: Structure-aware chunks beat fixed-size windows.
detail.hard: Big chunks buried the citation; small chunks lost the meaning. The overlap window was the compromise that made both work.
detail.say: Chunk size is a citation problem before it’s a retrieval problem.

iv.short: Databricks runs structural chunking as a batch job. It splits parsed documents on section boundaries instead of character counts, with an overlap tuned so a citation never straddles a chunk edge, and tags every chunk with domain, tier, date and type. Chunk size is a citation problem before it’s a retrieval problem.

qa.q: How did you choose the chunk size?
qa.a: Big chunks buried the citation; small chunks lost the meaning. Section-aware chunks with an overlap window were the compromise that made both work.
It’s batch compute over the whole corpus, and it’s where the Ontology Loader already runs, so chunking, stamping and the terminology build share one platform.

qa.q: What metadata does a chunk get?
qa.a: Domain, tier, date and type here; entity IDs, ancestor IDs and the vocabulary version at the stamping step. Those fields are what the search query filters on.

push.q: How would you know if chunking got worse?
push.a: Retrieval is evaluated on its own — RAGAS context precision and recall run on every chunking change — and a regression on any eval layer blocks the release.

detail.head: Where the ontology gets baked in: entity IDs plus the full ancestor set written onto every chunk.

Writes the entity IDs and the full ancestor set onto every chunk
This is the step that lets retrieval skip the graph entirely

detail.say: We pay the ontology cost once, at ingestion, instead of on every query.

It links mentions in each chunk to the terminology spine and writes the entity IDs, the full ancestor set and the vocabulary version onto the chunk, taken from the closure table. We pay the ontology cost once, at ingestion, instead of on every query.

qa.a: It’s what lets retrieval skip the graph entirely. Concept expansion becomes a filter on ancestor_ids, which is cheap and deterministic at query time.

qa.q: What happens when the vocabulary changes?
qa.a: A vocabulary release triggers a re-stamp of the affected chunks, so the index and the closure table are always the same version.

qa.q: How do you verify stamping is right?
qa.a: Closure-table fixtures: a parent-concept query must return the whole subtree, which only passes if the ancestors were stamped correctly.

push.q: Doesn’t re-stamping get expensive?
push.a: Only the affected chunks are re-stamped, and it’s a batch job on the ingestion side — never on the request path.

detail.head: Vectorizes chunks for the dense side of hybrid retrieval, with images verbalized first.
how: Batch pricing on the bulk ingestion workload
Re-embedding is a versioned, replayable job, not a manual rerun
detail.dh: Batch embedding with a recorded model version beat ad-hoc re-embedding.
detail.dec: Re-embedding the corpus is a pipeline run, not a project. The model version is recorded per chunk because mixing versions in one index is silently wrong.
detail.say: Re-embedding the corpus is a pipeline run, not a project.

iv.short: Embeddings vectorize each chunk for the dense side of hybrid retrieval, using text-embedding-3-large at batch pricing. Images are verbalized with AI Vision first, so they’re searchable as text. The model version is recorded on every chunk, because mixing embedding versions in one index is silently wrong. Re-embedding the corpus is a pipeline run, not a project.

qa.q: Why record the model version per chunk?
qa.a: Vectors from different embedding models aren’t comparable. If an index mixes versions, similarity scores are quietly wrong with no error to tell you. The version field lets us detect it and replay.

qa.q: How do you handle images and figures?
qa.a: AI Vision verbalizes them into text before embedding, so a figure’s content is retrievable like any other chunk.

qa.q: How would you switch embedding models?
qa.a: Re-embed as a versioned, replayable pipeline job at batch pricing, then rerun the retrieval eval — it runs on every index change — before the new vectors serve traffic.

push.q: Why not a domain-specific biomedical embedding model?
push.a: text-embedding-3-large runs inside our Azure OpenAI boundary with pinned deployments and Entra auth, which matters under change control, and BM25 plus ontology filters cover the exact biomedical terms. I’d evaluate a domain model on our retrieval set before switching.

detail.head: The batch job that produces the terminology artifacts — dictionary and closure table — per vocabulary release.
how: Runs on Databricks when the vocabulary spine changes
Builds the term dictionary and the ancestor closure as versioned release artifacts
A new vocabulary release triggers a re-stamp of affected chunks
detail.dh: A compile-time ontology beat a query-time one.
detail.dec: The alternative was a live graph database queried at request time. The loader makes the ontology a compile-time artifact instead: cheaper, deterministic, and validatable as a release.
detail.say: The ontology is built, versioned and released like code — not queried like a database.

iv.short: The Ontology Loader is a Databricks job that builds the terminology artifacts — the term dictionary and the closure table — whenever the vocabulary spine changes. Each build is a versioned release, and a new release re-stamps the affected chunks. The ontology is built, versioned and released like code, not queried like a database.

qa.q: Why treat the ontology as a build artifact?
qa.a: It’s cheaper, deterministic, and validatable as a release. A live graph queried at request time is none of those.
A change in the vocabulary spine — MedDRA, SNOMED CT or MeSH. The new release rebuilds both artifacts and re-stamps the affected chunks.
The dictionary goes to the Cosmos terminology container, read-only for the Ontology agent; the ancestors are stamped onto chunks in the index.

push.q: What if a vocabulary release is bad?
push.a: Each release is a versioned artifact, so rolling back means republishing the previous version and re-stamping — the same way we’d roll back code.

how: Immutable append of every request, retrieval set, citation and gate decision, by correlation ID
Includes the session context injected into each run, so nothing depends on Redis still holding it
Written on the path, not reconstructed from logs afterwards
This is what makes the platform defensible under 21 CFR Part 11 change control

detail.dec: If we cannot reconstruct why a scientist saw a specific sentence, the platform is not compliant. Cosmos is written as part of the request, including the session context that shaped the answer, so the record never depends on Redis.
detail.say: If we can’t reconstruct why a scientist saw a specific sentence, the platform isn’t compliant.

iv.short: Cosmos is the evidence record. By correlation ID it holds what was asked, what was retrieved, what was generated and what was shown — including the session context injected into each run. It’s written on the request path, not reconstructed from logs, under a custom append-only role. If we can’t reconstruct why a scientist saw a sentence, the platform isn’t compliant.

qa.q: Why write the audit trail on the request path?
qa.a: Because a record rebuilt from logs is only as complete as the logs. Written as part of the request, every claim resolves by correlation ID to its chunks, controlled versions, model deployment and verifier verdict.

qa.q: How do you make it tamper-resistant?

qa.q: Why not keep this in Redis?
qa.a: Redis keys expire and get evicted. Cosmos is the record, so the injected session context is written there too, and an answer can be reconstructed months later without Redis.
21 CFR Part 11 and GxP. Every model, prompt and index change is controlled, and every response is traceable to its evidence.

push.q: How would you answer an auditor?
push.a: Give me the correlation ID and I can show what was asked, which chunks and versions were retrieved, which model deployment generated the answer, what the verifier said, and what the user saw.

detail.head: One correlation ID from gateway through every agent hop and model call, plus the eval metrics.
how: Spans for retrieval, generation and each bus round trip
Makes a slow p95 attributable to a specific agent
detail.dh: Quality signals as first-class operational metrics beat infrastructure metrics alone.
detail.dec: Refusal rate and citation coverage move before CPU ever notices. They are alerted on like latency.
detail.hard: Open scientific Q&A has no single right answer, so no single metric is trustworthy. Seven partial views that all have to agree is the honest substitute for ground truth.
detail.say: When p95 moves, we know which agent moved it.

iv.short: Monitoring follows one correlation ID from the gateway through every agent hop and model call — OpenTelemetry into Application Insights, and Arize Phoenix for production LLM quality. The key idea: quality signals like refusal rate, citation coverage and retrieval hit rate are alerted on like latency, because they move before CPU ever notices.

qa.a: Gate failures and refusal-rate anomalies. Refusal rate is watched in both directions — a sudden drop usually means the gate broke. We also track citation coverage, retrieval hit rate, query drift, index staleness and per-agent latency SLOs.

qa.q: How do you find the cause of a slow p95?
qa.a: Per-agent spans on every retrieval, generation and bus round trip. When p95 moves, we know which agent moved it.

qa.q: How does monitoring connect to evaluation?
qa.a: Production monitoring is layer six of the seven-layer eval program. Open scientific Q&A has no single right answer, so seven partial views that all have to agree are the honest substitute for ground truth.
Spans record p50 and p95 tokens per agent, and those replace the engineering assumptions in the cost model.

push.q: What’s your ground truth?
push.a: There isn’t one for open scientific Q&A. That’s why no single metric is trusted — seven layers, from retrieval through SME review, have to agree, and SME findings feed the labeled eval sets.

Permissions are scoped per service: Search roles at index scope, Service Bus rights per topic and subscription. Purview covers data governance, and every change is controlled under Part 11 and GxP.

qa.q: What does change control look like?

bands.name: Query-time path — preprocess, retrieve in parallel, fuse, rerank, synthesize

detail.head: Everything that runs inside the latency budget, in five steps — one of which was added last.
how: Preprocess once, then both retrievers in parallel
Fuse on rank, rerank the top-K, synthesise only in Phase 3
detail.dh: Parallel retrieval with rank fusion beat a single retriever.
detail.dec: Both retrievers run on every request, so latency is the max of the two, not the sum. Fusion on rank position means no score normalization to tune and re-tune.
detail.say: The whole query path is five steps and one of them was added last.

iv.short: At query time there are five steps. Preprocessing resolves products, brands and SKUs, classifies intent and emits filters. FAISS and Elasticsearch then run in parallel, reciprocal rank fusion merges them by position, a cross-encoder reorders the top-K, and in Phase 3 GPT-3.5-Turbo writes a grounded answer. Retrieval through rerank stays under 900 ms at p95, at peak retail load.

qa.q: Why run both retrievers on every request?
qa.a: Because they fail differently. BM25 misses synonyms — “sheetrock” isn’t “drywall” — and dense retrieval is weaker on exact SKUs and model numbers. Running both in parallel means latency is the max of the two, not the sum.

qa.q: Why fuse on rank instead of score?
qa.a: A BM25 score and a cosine distance aren’t on comparable scales. We tried weighted score blending first, and any weighting learned on one query distribution failed on the next. Rank fusion has nothing to normalize.

qa.q: How do you hold the latency budget?
qa.a: FastAPI fans out asynchronously with a timeout per stage, so one slow leg can’t blow the p95. Per-stage latency is monitored, so a regression points at one stage.
Retrieval quality was already carrying the result. GPT-3.5-Turbo only became available on Azure in the final weeks, so it was layered on top of a ranking that was already measured and working.

push.q: If one retriever times out, what does the user get?
push.a: The other leg’s results. Each stage has its own timeout, so a slow retriever is cut off and fusion runs on what came back — a slightly weaker ranking instead of a missed p95.

Cosmos DB holds chunk metadata, lineage and ACL tags; PostgreSQL holds the result index, query logs and the relevance judgments behind the benchmarks.

qa.q: How do the ACL tags stay correct?
qa.a: They’re stamped once at ingestion and that exact tag is enforced at query time. One source of truth, so there’s no drift between what was indexed and what’s allowed.

qa.q: What did the query logs give you?
qa.a: They turned a hunch about synonyms into a measured share of traffic — and a business case. They also fed the judgment set and the failure analysis.

bands.name: Evaluation — the gate on every tuning decision

detail.head: The gate on every tuning decision: benchmark query sets and offline metrics.
how: Benchmark query sets curated per intent class with graded relevance judgments
NDCG@10 as the headline; MRR and MAP catch different failure shapes
Every fusion or reranker change replayed offline before rollout
A/B test on search success is the final decision
detail.dh: Replay against benchmarks beat tuning by feel.
detail.dec: Fusion weights and reranker changes were replayed against graded query sets before any rollout. Offline metrics bought permission to run the A/B test; search success decided.
detail.say: Tuning without a benchmark is guessing with extra steps.

iv.short: Evaluation was the gate on every tuning decision. We curated benchmark query sets per intent class with graded relevance judgments, scored every fusion or reranker change offline on NDCG@10, MRR and MAP, and only then ran a live A/B test on search success. Offline metrics bought permission to test; search success decided.

qa.a: It uses graded relevance and rewards putting the best results at the very top, and an associate on a handheld only looks at the first few. MRR and MAP catch different failure shapes — where the first good hit lands, and precision across all of them.
A single aggregate hides a regression on one intent class behind a gain on another. Per-class sets showed exactly where a change helped and where it hurt.
+14% NDCG@10 on the labeled set for hybrid plus rerank versus the BM25 control, and +21% search success in the live A/B test — sessions ending in a click-through or a resolved answer.

qa.q: Why not ship on offline metrics alone?
qa.a: Offline metrics predict; the A/B test decides. NDCG got us permission to run the test. Search success is what we shipped on.

push.q: What if NDCG went up but search success didn’t?
push.a: Search success wins — it’s the decision metric. Offline metrics only earn the right to run the test; if the live test doesn’t move, the change doesn’t ship.

bands.name: Ingestion / ETL — one document routed, chunked and embedded exactly once

detail.head: The batch path: route, extract, chunk, embed, dual-write — once per document version.
how: Document Sources land: PDF, DOCX, HTML, SharePoint, API feeds
File Type Router decides the handler on the bytes, not the filename
Extraction Handlers emit one normalized shape
Split & Chunk with spaCy sentences, recursive with overlap
Embeddings computed in-cluster, 768-dim
Dual-Write to both indexes, idempotent and versioned
detail.dh: Idempotent, versioned dual-write beat two independent indexing jobs.
detail.dec: Both indexes are derived from one versioned chunk set, so they cannot disagree about what a document says.
detail.say: One document, routed, chunked and embedded exactly once.

iv.short: Ingestion is the batch path: five source types — PDF, DOCX, HTML, SharePoint and API feeds — about 1,200 documents a week. A router picks the handler from the file’s bytes, each handler emits one normalized shape, sentence-aware chunking keeps steps and spec tables whole, all-mpnet-base-v2 embeds in-cluster, and a versioned dual-write puts every chunk into both FAISS and Elasticsearch, once.

qa.q: Why dual-write from one chunk set?
qa.a: The two indexes drifting apart — one rebuilt, one not — produced the most confusing bugs on the platform. Writing both from one versioned chunk set means they can’t disagree about what a document says.

qa.q: How do you handle a catalog that never sits still?
qa.a: New SKUs arrived with thin, inconsistent text and got weak embeddings. The fix was to normalize and enrich before embedding, plus a state-tracked refresh path — not a better model.
Embedding live inventory. Anything that changes hourly should be looked up, not retrieved — freshness beats semantics for a stock count.
Files lie about what they are. A .pdf that’s really HTML silently produces an empty chunk set unless the router checks the MIME type, so unknown types are quarantined, not guessed.

push.q: Is re-running a batch safe?
push.a: Yes. Dual-write is idempotent and versioned, so the same version gives the same result.

detail.head: Store associates on the floor and merchandising analysts — two very different users of one search box.
how: Associates need an answer in the aisle, in seconds, on a handheld
Analysts need coverage: every spec, every guide, every playbook
detail.dh: One index for both audiences beat two products.
detail.dec: The associate case set the latency budget; the analyst case set the coverage requirement. Serving both from one hybrid index was the whole point.
detail.say: Two audiences, one index. The associate case is what set the latency budget.

iv.short: Two very different users of one search box: store associates, who need an answer in the aisle in seconds on a handheld, and merchandising analysts, who need coverage — every spec, guide and playbook. The associate case set the latency budget; the analyst case set the coverage requirement.

qa.q: Why one index for both audiences?
qa.a: Serving both from one hybrid index was the whole point. Before this, associates jumped across systems — specs, DIY guides, store-ops playbooks, live inventory — to answer a single customer question.

qa.q: How did the two users shape the design?
qa.a: The associate on a handheld set the p95 budget under 900 ms. The analyst who needs everything set the coverage bar, which is why BM25 stayed for exact SKUs while dense retrieval handled intent.

qa.q: How did you measure success for them?
qa.a: +21% search success in the live A/B test — sessions ending in a click-through or a resolved answer — and +14% NDCG@10 offline.

push.q: Do associates and analysts see the same content?
push.a: No. Role-based access applies inside the query, so store-ops content is filtered by role — the permission is a property of the search, not the UI.

detail.head: Authentication and role-based access in front of the search API.
how: Store-ops content is filtered by role at query time
detail.dh: Role filters applied to the query beat filtering the results page.
detail.dec: Store-ops content is filtered by role at query time. The permission is a property of the search, not of the UI.
detail.say: The permission is applied to the query, not to the results page.

iv.short: The API gateway authenticates the caller with TSC Identity and applies role-based access before the search API. Store-ops content is filtered by role at query time — the permission is a property of the search, not of the results page.

qa.q: Why apply the role to the query and not the UI?
qa.a: If the UI hides results, the content was still retrieved, ranked and sent. Applying the role as a query filter means the search never touches what the user can’t see.
TSC Identity issues the caller’s token, and RBAC policy feeds decide what each role can see.

qa.q: How does that connect to ingestion?
qa.a: The ACL tag captured when a document is indexed is the same tag enforced at query time, so permissions have one source of truth.

detail.head: The service the storefront and associate tools call — async fan-out with a timeout per stage.
how: Async fan-out to both retrievers
Timeout budget enforced per stage so one slow leg cannot blow the p95
detail.dh: A per-stage timeout budget beat one global timeout.
detail.dec: Every stage has its own timeout, so one slow leg cannot blow the p95. The budget is enforced, not hoped for.
detail.say: Every stage has its own timeout. The p95 is a budget, not a hope.

iv.short: FastAPI is the service the storefront and associate tools call. It fans out asynchronously to both retrievers and enforces a timeout per stage, so one slow leg can’t blow the p95. The budget is enforced, not hoped for.

qa.q: Why per-stage timeouts instead of one global timeout?
qa.a: A global timeout only tells you the request was slow. Per-stage timeouts stop one slow retriever from eating the whole budget, and per-stage latency tells you which stage regressed.
Async fan-out to two retrievers is the heart of the request, and FastAPI on Python made that natural while sitting next to the spaCy and sentence-transformers code.
The ranked results — and in Phase 3, a synthesized answer with every claim cited and resolvable to its chunks and index version.

push.a: The p95 held under 900 milliseconds, retrieval through rerank, measured at peak retail load.

iv.short: Three delivery phases — a BM25 foundation, hybrid retrieval, then RAG synthesis. Five source types, about 1,200 documents a week, two retrieval indexes fused by rank. The result: plus 14% NDCG@10, plus 21% search success, and p95 under 900 milliseconds.

qa.a: September 2021 to mid 2022: unify the content and prove a BM25 baseline, with a FAISS prototype. Mid 2022 to early 2023: production hybrid search with RRF and a cross-encoder, validated in an A/B test. Then March to April 2023: GPT-3.5-Turbo synthesis on top.

Each phase had a gate before the next one started: unified search had to beat associates juggling systems, and hybrid had to beat lexical live and inside the latency budget. Phasing kept the timeline honest.

push.q: Why GPT-3.5 and not something newer?
push.a: That’s what Azure hosted at the time — gpt-35-turbo arrived in preview in the final weeks, March to April 2023. Synthesis sits on top of retrieval as its own layer, so the model is swappable.
