detail.head: Turns a raw query into a resolved query plus filters before either index sees it.
detail.role: The incoming search.
how: Short, ambiguous and full of trade vocabulary
Roughly half the queries contain a term the catalog spells differently
detail.dh: Preprocessing once beat letting each retriever interpret the query.
detail.dec: Intent classification and SKU extraction happen once and feed both retrievers the same resolved query and filter set. That is what keeps the two candidate lists comparable.
detail.say: "Sheetrock" isn’t "drywall," and the customer is not going to change.

iv.short: Query preprocessing turns a raw query into a resolved query plus filters before either index sees it. spaCy NER pulls out products, brands and SKUs, a classifier assigns one of four intent classes, and semantic rewriting normalizes trade vocabulary. Both retrievers get the same resolved query, which keeps their candidate lists comparable.

qa.q: Why preprocess once instead of per retriever?
qa.a: So both retrievers see the same resolved query and filter set. If each interpreted the query its own way, the two candidate lists wouldn’t be comparable at fusion.
Vocabulary mismatch. Roughly half the queries contained a term the catalog spells differently — “sheetrock” isn’t “drywall,” and the customer isn’t going to change.
The filters, and the evaluation: benchmark sets were curated per intent class, so a regression on one class showed up even when the average improved.

push.q: Why not just add a synonym list to Elasticsearch?
push.a: Synonym lists help BM25 for the terms you’ve thought of; they don’t cover intent-based queries phrased in a shopper’s own words. Dense retrieval covers those, and preprocessing normalizes what it can before either index runs.

detail.head: The dense half: recovers intent-based queries where the shopper’s words don’t match the catalog’s.
how: Approximate nearest-neighbour over the 768-dim vectors
Tuned for recall, since the reranker fixes ordering downstream
detail.dh: IVF-PQ tuned for recall beat exact search — the reranker fixes ordering.
detail.dec: Dense retrieval buys recall on vocabulary mismatch. Precision is the reranker’s job, so FAISS is tuned for recall and speed rather than exactness.
detail.say: Dense retrieval buys recall. Precision is the reranker’s job.

iv.short: FAISS is the dense half. It runs approximate nearest-neighbour search over 768-dimensional vectors with an IVF-PQ index, and it recovers intent-based queries where the shopper’s words don’t match the catalog’s. It’s tuned for recall and speed, because ordering is the reranker’s job.

qa.q: Why IVF-PQ rather than exact search?
qa.a: Dense retrieval buys recall on vocabulary mismatch. Precision is the reranker’s job, so FAISS is tuned for recall and speed rather than exactness.

qa.q: What does dense retrieval catch that BM25 misses?
qa.a: Intent and synonyms — queries whose words never appear in the catalog. In the POC, the FAISS prototype recovered intent-based queries BM25 missed, and that’s what greenlit hybrid.

qa.q: Where do the vectors come from?
qa.a: all-mpnet-base-v2, self-hosted in-cluster, 768 dimensions, with the model version recorded per chunk.

push.q: Doesn’t PQ compression hurt quality?
push.a: It trades some exactness for speed and memory. That’s acceptable because FAISS only has to get the right documents into the candidate set — the cross-encoder fixes the order of the top-K.

nodes.name: Elasticsearch BM25
nodes.sub:
inverted index · TF weighting
exact SKU / model match

detail.head: The lexical half: still the best thing in the system for an exact SKU or model number.
how: Exact-match and rare-term recall
Built first, as the Phase 1 baseline everything else was measured against
detail.dh: Keeping BM25 beat replacing it with dense retrieval.
detail.dec: Dense retrieval was added next to BM25, never instead of it. Exact identifiers and rare terms are where lexical search still wins outright.
detail.say: We never replaced BM25. Dense retrieval was added next to it, not instead of it.

iv.short: Elasticsearch BM25 is the lexical half, and still the best thing in the system for an exact SKU or model number. It was built first, as the Phase 1 baseline everything else was measured against, and we never replaced it — dense retrieval was added next to it, not instead of it.

qa.q: Why keep BM25 once you had dense retrieval?
qa.a: Exact identifiers and rare terms are where lexical search still wins outright. A SKU or a model number needs an exact match, not a nearest neighbour.
It’s blind to synonyms — “sheetrock” isn’t “drywall.” That’s the gap dense recall filled.
It was the baseline. The POC had to prove that one lexical search over all the content beat associates juggling systems, and every later change was measured against BM25 as the control.

push.q: Why not tune BM25 harder instead of adding vectors?
push.a: We measured the gap first: the dense prototype recovered intent-based queries BM25 missed, and roughly half of queries had a vocabulary mismatch. That’s a recall problem BM25 can’t tune its way out of.

detail.head: Merges the two candidate lists by rank position rather than by score.
how: Reciprocal rank fusion with k=60
No score normalization, no tuning per query type
detail.dh: Rank fusion beat weighted score blending.
detail.dec: Weighted score blending was tried first and abandoned. A BM25 score and a cosine distance are not on a comparable scale, and any weighting learned on one query distribution failed on the next.
detail.hard: The fusion step is where most hybrid search implementations quietly go wrong. Rank is comparable; raw score is not.
detail.say: We fuse on rank, not on score, because the two scores don’t live in the same space.

iv.short: Reciprocal rank fusion merges the two candidate lists by rank position, not by score, with k equal to 60. There’s no score normalization and no tuning per query type, because a BM25 score and a cosine distance don’t live in the same space.

qa.a: Weighted score blending. A BM25 score and a cosine distance aren’t on comparable scales, and any weighting learned on one query distribution failed on the next. We abandoned it.
Each document scores the sum of one over k plus its rank in each list. Documents both retrievers rank well rise to the top, and there are no raw scores to calibrate.
It’s the standard constant from the original RRF work. It damps the advantage of a single top rank, so agreement between the two retrievers counts for more.

push.q: Where do hybrid systems usually go wrong?
push.a: At fusion. Rank is comparable; raw score is not. That’s where most hybrid search implementations quietly go wrong.

detail.head: Reads query and candidate together and reorders the top-K.
how: Applied to the top candidates only — it is too expensive for the full list
This is where "related but not what I wanted" gets pushed back down
detail.dh: Reranking the top-K beat reranking everything — and beat not reranking.
detail.dec: Fusion got the right documents into the set; it did not get them in the right order. The cross-encoder is what turned recall into a visible improvement — applied to the top-K only, because it is too expensive for the full list.
detail.hard: Fusion got the right documents into the candidate set; it did not get them in the right order. The reranker is what turned recall into a visible improvement for associates.
detail.say: Fusion fixed recall. The cross-encoder fixed the top three results, which is all anyone looks at.

iv.short: The cross-encoder, ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2, reads the query and each candidate together and reorders the top-K. Fusion got the right documents into the set; it didn’t get them in the right order. The reranker turned recall into a visible improvement — on the top-K only, because it’s too expensive for the full list.

qa.a: Fused candidates surfaced related-but-not-wanted items near the top. The cross-encoder pushes true intent up — and the top three results are all anyone looks at.
A cross-encoder scores every query-candidate pair jointly, so cost grows with each candidate. Applying it to the top-K keeps it inside the latency budget.
ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 is small enough to run inside the p95 budget and trained for passage ranking.

push.q: How much of the gain came from reranking versus fusion?
push.a: The +14% is hybrid plus rerank together, against BM25. Qualitatively, fusion fixed recall and the cross-encoder fixed the order of the top results.

detail.head: Composes a direct answer over reranked context. The last thing built, not the first.
how: Strictly grounded on reranked passages
Falls back to the ranked result list when grounding is thin
Arrived only when Azure hosted gpt-35-turbo, in the final weeks
detail.dh: Building synthesis last beat building it first.
detail.dec: Retrieval quality was already carrying the result before GPT-3.5-Turbo was available on Azure. Grounding strictly on reranked context, with a fallback to the ranked list, kept synthesis from drifting.
detail.hard: Synthesis can over-summarize and drift from the source. The answer quality watch is on the synthesis layer specifically, separately from ranking metrics.
detail.say: Retrieval quality was already carrying the result before synthesis existed. That ordering was deliberate.

iv.short: RAG synthesis composes a direct answer over the reranked context with GPT-3.5-Turbo, in Phase 3 only. It’s strictly grounded on reranked passages and falls back to the ranked result list when grounding is thin. It was the last thing built, not the first — retrieval quality was already carrying the result.

qa.a: GPT-3.5-Turbo only became available on Azure in the final weeks, but the order was also deliberate: synthesis is only as good as the retrieval underneath it, and retrieval was already measured and working.

qa.q: How do you keep answers grounded?
qa.a: The model only sees reranked passages, every claim is cited, and when grounding is thin it falls back to the ranked result list instead of answering.
Synthesis can over-summarize and drift from the source. Answer quality was watched on the synthesis layer specifically, separately from the ranking metrics.

push.q: What happens when the answer would be weak?
push.a: It degrades to search results, not to a guess. Thin grounding falls back to the ranked list, which was already measured and trusted.

detail.head: The two models the query path calls: the self-hosted embedder and, in Phase 3, GPT-3.5-Turbo.
detail.role: Self-hosted sentence-transformers for dense retrieval.
how: 768-dimension vectors, served in-house
Document content never leaves the security boundary
Hosted embeddings arrived on Azure late in the engagement and were treated as a migration, not the starting point
detail.dh: Self-hosted embeddings beat a hosted embedding API.
detail.dec: A hosted embedding API is less to operate. Self-hosting won on two grounds: it was what actually existed for most of this timeline, and it kept content inside the ISO 27001 boundary.
detail.say: Self-hosted SBERT — period-correct, and it kept the corpus inside the boundary.

iv.short: The model layer is the two models the query path calls: all-mpnet-base-v2, self-hosted, for 768-dimensional embeddings, and in Phase 3, GPT-3.5-Turbo for synthesis. Self-hosting the embedder kept document content inside the ISO 27001 boundary, and it was what actually existed for most of this timeline.

qa.a: Two reasons: it was the period-correct enterprise SBERT stack for most of 2021 to 2023, and it kept content inside the ISO 27001 boundary. A hosted API would have been less to operate.

qa.q: What happened when hosted embeddings became available?
qa.a: They arrived on Azure late in the engagement and were treated as a migration, not the starting point.

qa.q: Where is the embedder called on the query path?
qa.a: Once, during preprocessing. The vector then goes to FAISS.

push.q: Would you self-host today?
push.a: It depends on the boundary. If a hosted embedding service runs inside the same security boundary with pinned versions, I’d take it — and treat the switch as a re-embedding migration with a retrieval eval before cutover.

detail.head: Chunk metadata, lineage and the ACL tags that become query-time filters.
detail.role: Query, click and session logging.
how: Feeds the judgment set and the failure analysis
Where "vocabulary mismatch" stopped being an anecdote and became a measured share of traffic
detail.dh: Stamping ACL at ingestion beat looking it up at query time.
detail.dec: The tag captured when a document is indexed is the tag enforced when it is searched. One source of truth, no drift between what was indexed and what is allowed.
detail.say: The logs are what turned a hunch about synonyms into a business case.

iv.short: Cosmos DB holds chunk metadata, lineage and ACL tags — the tags that become query-time filters. The ACL captured when a document is indexed is the ACL enforced when it’s searched, so there’s one source of truth and no drift between what was indexed and what’s allowed.

qa.a: So the query can filter on them directly. Looking permissions up at query time adds latency and a second source of truth that can drift.
Every answer resolves to the chunks it cited, the index version they came from and the embedding model that produced them.

qa.q: How do filters reach the indexes?
qa.a: Department, doc type and ACL travel with every chunk and are applied as filters inside both the FAISS and the Elasticsearch query.

push.q: What if a document’s permissions change?
push.a: The tag is part of the chunk’s metadata, so a permission change is a re-ingestion of that document — and the dual-write updates both indexes together.

detail.head: Relational store for the result index, query logs and relevance judgments.
detail.role: Relational store for catalog metadata and index state.
how: Tracks what has been indexed, at what version, and what needs refresh
detail.dh: Logging every query beat sampling.
detail.dec: The logs are what turned a hunch about synonyms into a measured share of traffic — and a business case.
detail.say: The refresh path is state-tracked, so a failed load doesn’t silently leave a stale index.

iv.short: PostgreSQL is the relational store for the result index, query logs and relevance judgments. It tracks what’s been indexed, at which version, and what needs refresh — and every query is logged, which is what turned a hunch about synonyms into a measured share of traffic.

qa.q: Why log every query instead of sampling?
qa.a: Because the failure we cared about — vocabulary mismatch — only shows up as a share of traffic. Logging everything turned a hunch into a business case and fed the judgment set.

qa.q: How does it keep the index fresh?
qa.a: The refresh path is state-tracked, so a failed load doesn’t silently leave a stale index.
Graded human relevance labels on real queries, curated per intent class — the set every ranking change is scored against.

push.q: How do you know an index is stale?
push.a: PostgreSQL records what has been indexed and at which version, so a document whose latest version isn’t in the index shows up as needing refresh.

detail.head: Graded query sets, curated per intent class, that every tuning change is scored against.
detail.role: The labeled judgment set every ranking change is measured against.
how: Built from real queries with human relevance labels
Any ranking change is scored offline before it goes near an A/B test
detail.dh: Curated per-class sets beat one aggregate benchmark.
detail.dec: A single aggregate hides a regression on one intent class behind a gain on another. Per-class sets showed exactly where a change helped and where it hurt.
detail.say: No ranking change ships without a number attached to it.

iv.short: The benchmark query sets are graded relevance judgments on real queries, curated per intent class. Every fusion or reranker change was scored against them offline before it went anywhere near an A/B test. No ranking change shipped without a number attached.

qa.a: A single aggregate hides a regression on one intent class behind a gain on another. Per-class sets showed exactly where a change helped and where it hurt.

qa.q: Where did the queries come from?
qa.a: Real queries from the logs, with human relevance labels.
Every fusion-weight and reranker change was replayed against them before rollout, scored on NDCG@10, MRR and MAP.

push.q: Tuning by feel is faster — why bother?
push.a: Tuning without a benchmark is guessing with extra steps. The per-class replay is what let us prove the +14% and justify the live test.

detail.head: The offline gate on every tuning decision.
detail.role: Live validation on actual shoppers.
how: Search success — click-through or resolved answer — is the decision metric
Offline metrics predict; the A/B test decides
detail.dh: Offline metrics as a gate beat offline metrics as a report.
detail.say: NDCG got us permission to run the test. Search success is what we shipped on.

iv.short: Offline metrics were the gate on every tuning decision: NDCG@10 as the headline, with MRR and MAP catching different failure shapes. They predict; the A/B test decides. NDCG got us permission to run the test — search success is what we shipped on.

qa.q: What’s the difference between NDCG, MRR and MAP?
qa.a: NDCG rewards ranking the most relevant results highest, using graded labels. MRR looks at where the first relevant result lands. MAP averages precision across all the relevant results. Each catches a different way a ranking can fail.

qa.q: What was the live decision metric?
qa.a: Search success: the share of sessions ending in a click-through or a resolved answer — up 21% in the A/B test.

qa.q: Did you keep measuring after launch?
qa.a: Yes. Ranking quality was monitored continuously on NDCG, MRR and MAP, because it drifts with the catalog.

push.q: Isn’t click-through a noisy success signal?
push.a: On its own, yes. That’s why search success counted a click-through or a resolved answer, and why graded offline judgments gated every change before it reached the live test.

nodes.name: Document Sources
nodes.sub:
PDF · DOCX · HTML
SharePoint · API feeds

detail.head: Five source types — specs, DIY guides, store-ops playbooks, live inventory — at ~1,200 documents a week.
detail.role: Product specification sheets and buying guides — the densest and most-cited content in the corpus.
how: ~1,200 documents a week across all sources
Specs are table-heavy, which drives the parsing approach
detail.dh: Looking up live inventory beat embedding it.
detail.dec: Anything that changes hourly should be looked up, not retrieved. Embedding inventory was a mistake worth not repeating.
detail.hard: Embedding live inventory was a mistake worth not repeating. Freshness beats semantics for a stock count.
detail.say: Most of what an associate needs is in a spec table, not in prose.

iv.short: Five source types — PDF, DOCX, HTML, SharePoint and API feeds — covering product specs, DIY guides, store-ops playbooks and live inventory, at about 1,200 documents a week. Spec sheets are the densest, most-cited content, and they’re table-heavy, which drove the parsing approach.

qa.q: What was the mistake worth not repeating?
qa.a: Embedding live inventory. Anything that changes hourly should be looked up, not retrieved — freshness beats semantics for a stock count.

qa.q: Why does content type matter so much?
qa.a: Most of what an associate needs is in a spec table, not in prose. That’s why tables are kept intact through extraction and chunking.
About 1,200 documents a week across all five source types.

push.q: So how was inventory answered?
push.a: As a live lookup rather than retrieval. Inventory changes hourly, so it should be looked up, not embedded.

detail.head: Decides which extraction handler a document goes to — on the bytes, not the filename.
how: python-magic on the MIME type first
Falls back to extension, then to header sniffing
Unknown types are quarantined, not guessed
detail.dh: MIME sniffing beat trusting the extension.
detail.hard: Files lie about what they are. A .pdf that is actually HTML will silently produce an empty chunk set unless the router checks the bytes.
detail.say: Route on the bytes, not the filename.

iv.short: The file type router decides which extraction handler a document goes to — on the bytes, not the filename. python-magic checks the MIME type first, then falls back to the extension and header sniffing, and unknown types are quarantined, not guessed.

qa.q: Why not trust the file extension?
qa.a: Files lie about what they are. A .pdf that’s actually HTML silently produces an empty chunk set unless the router checks the bytes.

qa.q: What happens to an unknown type?
qa.a: It’s quarantined, not guessed, so a bad file can’t quietly produce empty or garbage chunks.

qa.q: Why does this matter for search quality?
qa.a: An empty chunk set doesn’t raise an error — the document just disappears from search. Catching it at routing is far cheaper than finding it from a missing result.

detail.head: One handler per format, each producing the same normalized text plus metadata.
how: PyMuPDF for text PDFs, pdfplumber where tables matter
python-docx, BeautifulSoup for HTML, OCR as the last resort
detail.dh: A common output shape beat format-specific pipelines.
detail.dec: Every handler emits the same shape, so everything downstream is format-blind. Adding a format is one handler, not a new pipeline.
detail.say: Every handler emits the same shape, so everything downstream is format-blind.

iv.short: Extraction has one handler per format, and each emits the same normalized text plus metadata: PyMuPDF for text PDFs, pdfplumber where tables matter, python-docx, BeautifulSoup for HTML, and OCR as the last resort. Everything downstream is format-blind.

qa.a: Adding a format becomes one handler, not a new pipeline, and chunking, embedding and indexing never need to know where a document came from.
PyMuPDF is fast for text PDFs; pdfplumber is used where tables matter, and spec sheets are table-heavy.
Last resort — for scanned documents, after the text-based handlers.

detail.head: Splits guides and specs into retrievable passages that keep their context.
how: Keeps spec tables intact
Section-aware splits so a step in a DIY guide keeps its context
detail.dh: Sentence-aware recursive chunking beat fixed windows.
detail.dec: A how-to step retrieved without its preceding step is worse than no result. spaCy sentence boundaries plus overlap keep steps and spec tables whole.
detail.hard: New SKUs arrived with thin, inconsistent text and got weak embeddings. Enriching before embedding was the fix, not a better model.
detail.say: A how-to step retrieved without its preceding step is worse than no result.

iv.short: Split and chunk turns guides and specs into retrievable passages that keep their context. spaCy sentence boundaries plus recursive splitting with overlap keep a DIY step with the step before it, and spec tables intact. A how-to step retrieved without its preceding step is worse than no result.

qa.a: They cut steps and tables in half. Sentence-aware recursive chunking with overlap keeps each step and each spec table whole.

qa.q: What went wrong with new SKUs?
qa.a: They arrived with thin, inconsistent text and got weak embeddings. The fix was enriching the text before embedding, not a better model.
They’re kept intact as one unit, because the spec table is usually the answer.

push.q: How did you choose the chunk size?
push.a: By replaying it against the benchmark sets — scoring chunking choices on the same NDCG and MRR as ranking changes.

detail.head: Self-hosted sentence-transformers for dense retrieval, in-cluster.
how: 768-dimension vectors, served in-house
Document content never leaves the security boundary
Hosted embeddings arrived on Azure late in the engagement and were treated as a migration, not the starting point
detail.dh: Self-hosted SBERT beat a hosted embedding API.
detail.dec: A hosted embedding API is less to operate. Self-hosting won on two grounds: it was what actually existed for most of this timeline, and it kept content inside the ISO 27001 boundary.
detail.say: Self-hosted SBERT — period-correct, and it kept the corpus inside the boundary.

iv.short: Embeddings come from all-mpnet-base-v2, self-hosted in-cluster, producing 768-dimensional vectors. Document content never leaves the security boundary. Hosted embeddings arrived on Azure late in the engagement and were treated as a migration, not the starting point.

qa.a: It was what actually existed for most of this timeline, and it kept the corpus inside the ISO 27001 boundary. Period-correct and secure.

qa.q: How do you handle an embedding model change?
qa.a: The model version is recorded per chunk, so a change is a versioned re-embed, not a silent mix of vectors in one index.

qa.q: How do new products get good embeddings?
qa.a: Normalize and enrich their text first. Thin SKU text produced weak vectors no matter the model.

push.q: Wasn’t a hosted API simpler?
push.a: Less to operate, yes. Self-hosting won because it existed for most of the timeline and it kept the corpus inside the ISO 27001 boundary.

detail.head: Writes every chunk into both indexes, idempotently, with a version.
how: Both indexes rebuilt independently from the same chunk set
Re-running a batch is safe: same version, same result
detail.dh: Versioned dual-write beat two independent index jobs.
detail.hard: The two indexes drifting apart — one rebuilt, one not — produced the most confusing bugs on the platform. Versioned dual-write is what stopped it.
detail.say: Both indexes are derived from one versioned chunk set, so they cannot disagree about what a document says.

iv.short: Dual-write puts every chunk into both FAISS and Elasticsearch, idempotently and with a version. Both indexes are derived from one versioned chunk set, so they can’t disagree about what a document says — and re-running a batch is safe: same version, same result.

qa.a: The two indexes drifting apart — one rebuilt, one not — produced the most confusing bugs on the platform. Versioned dual-write is what stopped it.
Re-running a batch writes the same version and produces the same result, so retries and replays are safe.

qa.q: Can you rebuild one index alone?
qa.a: Yes — each index can be rebuilt independently from the same versioned chunk set.

push.q: What if one write succeeds and the other fails?
push.a: The version makes it detectable and the write is idempotent, so the batch is simply re-run until both indexes hold the same version.

detail.head: Where state and lineage live — every answer resolves to its chunks, index version and embedding model.
how: Embedding model version recorded per chunk
Every answer resolves to the chunks it cited and the index version they came from
detail.dh: Recording the embedding model per chunk beat assuming one version.
detail.say: Every answer resolves to its chunks, its index version and the embedding model that produced them.

iv.short: Storage and lineage is where state lives — Cosmos DB and PostgreSQL — with the embedding model version recorded per chunk. Every answer resolves to the chunks it cited, the index version they came from, and the embedding model that produced them.

qa.q: Why record the embedding model per chunk?
qa.a: Vectors from different models aren’t comparable. Recording the version means a migration can’t silently mix them in one index.

qa.q: What can you reconstruct for an answer?
qa.a: Its cited chunks, the index version they came from, and the embedding model that produced them.

qa.q: How did that help the hosted-embedding migration?
qa.a: Because each chunk carries its model version, moving to hosted embeddings could be a tracked re-embed rather than a big-bang switch.

detail.head: Operational monitoring across retrieval, ranking and serving.
how: Per-stage latency so a p95 regression is attributable
Ranking quality tracked continuously, not just at release
detail.dh: Continuous ranking-quality monitoring beat testing only at release.
detail.dec: Ranking quality drifts with the catalog. Per-stage latency makes a p95 regression attributable to one stage.
detail.say: Ranking quality drifts with the catalog. It needs monitoring, not just testing.

iv.short: Observability covers retrieval, ranking and serving: Elasticsearch into Kibana for logs, Prometheus and Grafana for metrics. Per-stage latency makes a p95 regression attributable to one stage, and ranking quality is tracked continuously, because it drifts with the catalog.

qa.a: The catalog never sits still, so ranking quality drifts. Testing only at release would miss that.

qa.q: How do you debug a p95 regression?
qa.a: Per-stage latency points at the stage — preprocessing, either retriever, fusion, rerank or synthesis.
Latency per stage against the SLO, and ranking quality — NDCG and MRR — tracked over time.

push.q: How do you measure ranking quality without production labels?
push.a: Against the benchmark judgment sets on a schedule, plus the live search-success signal from sessions.

nodes.name: Security & Governance
nodes.sub: TSC Identity · RBAC policy feeds · ISO 27001

detail.head: Identity, role policy and the boundary the self-hosted decision protected.
how: TSC Identity issues the caller token; RBAC policy feeds decide what a role can see
ISO 27001 boundary is why embeddings ran in-cluster
detail.dh: Keeping content in-cluster beat convenience.
detail.say: Self-hosting the embedder was a security decision before it was a cost decision.

iv.short: Security and governance: TSC Identity issues the caller token, RBAC policy feeds decide what each role can see, and the ISO 27001 boundary is why embeddings ran in-cluster. Self-hosting the embedder was a security decision before it was a cost decision.

qa.a: The token identifies the caller, RBAC decides the role’s scope, and that scope is applied as a filter inside the search query — not on the results page.

qa.q: What did ISO 27001 change about the architecture?
qa.a: It’s why the embedder was self-hosted: document content never left the security boundary.
Captured at ingestion as tags on each chunk, and enforced at query time from those same tags.

push.q: Did GPT-3.5-Turbo break that boundary?
push.a: It ran on Azure in Phase 3, and it only ever saw the reranked passages the user was already allowed to retrieve.

edges: parallel dispatch — both indexes on every request
fusion weights + reranker replayed against benchmarks before rollout

trace.text: 1 / 5 — An associate or analyst hits the API Gateway; TSC Identity issues the token and RBAC decides what their role can see. FastAPI owns the per-stage timeout budget.
2 / 5 — Preprocessing resolves products, brands and SKUs, classifies intent, rewrites the query and emits the filter set. The embedder is called once here.
3 / 5 — Parallel dispatch: FAISS for semantic recall, Elasticsearch for exact SKU and model matches, both with department, doc-type and ACL filters applied in the query.
4 / 5 — Reciprocal rank fusion merges by position, the cross-encoder reorders the top-K. Every change to either was replayed against the benchmarks before rollout.
5 / 5 — Phase 3 only: GPT-3.5-Turbo synthesises over reranked context and the answer returns through FastAPI, every claim cited, resolvable to its chunks and index version.

sheet.title: Real-Time Fraud Detection — MLOps Reference Architecture
sheet.sub: Citibank · AWS · governed under SR 11-7 model risk management

bands.name: DATA PLANE · FEATURES AND LABELS

detail.head: Where authorization events become features and late labels become a training set.
detail.role: Where the data comes from and how it becomes labels and a training set.
how: Authorization events stream in from MSK / Kinesis alongside S3, RDS, device and merchant context
Ingest tokenizes PII and attaches lineage and governance checks
Stream Feature Compute derives velocity, entity and device counters
Feature Store writes online and offline from one definition
Label Store joins chargeback outcomes back to transactions
Curated Training Set does a point-in-time correct join with time-based splits
detail.dh: One feature definition for both stores beat separate online and offline pipelines.
detail.dec: Training-serving skew was the most expensive class of bug. Computing features once on the stream and writing both stores from one definition removed it.
detail.say: The data plane is where point-in-time correctness is won or lost.

iv.short: The fraud data plane turns authorization events into features, and late labels into a training set. Auth events stream from MSK and Kinesis alongside the S3 lake, RDS, device and merchant context. Ingest tokenizes PII and attaches lineage, Flink computes velocity and entity counters, the feature store writes online and offline from one definition, and the label store joins chargebacks back 30 to 90 days later.

qa.q: What was the most expensive class of bug?
qa.a: Training-serving skew — a feature computed one way in a notebook and another way in serving changes model behavior in production with no code change anywhere. Computing features once on the stream and writing both stores from one definition removed it.

qa.q: How do late labels change the design?
qa.a: Chargebacks land 30 to 90 days after the transaction, so the training set is a point-in-time correct join with time-based splits. A random split would leak the future.
Fraud is scored inside the authorization window, so velocity and entity counters have to come from the stream. Slower context — device, merchant, customer — joins from the lake.

push.q: How do you guarantee point-in-time correctness?
push.a: A training row only sees what was knowable at that moment: features and labels are joined as of the transaction time, and the training set is immutable and versioned so it can be rebuilt.

bands.name: BUILD AND PROMOTION · THE GOVERNANCE SPINE

detail.head: The governance spine — the same six stages on every Citibank workload.
how: Notebooks become production scripts, built and versioned by Jenkins with Terraform IaC
One immutable image digest promoted dev → UAT → production
Train, evaluate, package, register — nothing reaches an endpoint outside this path
detail.dh: One governed path to production beat per-team pipelines.
detail.dec: Three very different model shapes share one promotion path. That is what let model risk validate the pipeline once and trust every model that comes through it.
detail.say: One governance spine serving three very different model shapes.

iv.short: Every Citibank workload — fraud, credit and AML — goes through the same governance spine. Notebooks become production scripts, Jenkins builds and versions them with Terraform for the infrastructure, one immutable image digest is promoted from dev to UAT to production, and SageMaker trains, evaluates, packages and registers into MLflow. Nothing reaches an endpoint outside this path.

qa.q: Why one path for three very different models?
qa.a: It let model risk validate the pipeline once and trust every model that comes through it. Fraud, credit and AML have very different shapes, but the promotion path, the lineage and the gates are the same.

qa.q: What did governance look like before?
qa.a: Models lived on laptops with governance by spreadsheet, and validators were reconstructing models instead of validating them. Getting models off laptops was the whole first phase.

qa.q: How do you prove a model is reproducible?
qa.a: Lineage is captured at train time — data version, code and params — and training data is immutable and versioned. The POC gate was rebuilding a model from its record alone, and model risk accepted it.
100% of deployments carry lineage: every endpoint traces to its data version, code commit, params and the validation record that cleared it.

push.q: Doesn’t one path slow every team down to the speed of review?
push.a: The review queue was the real bottleneck, and bottlenecks breed shortcuts. We didn’t validate less — the pipeline packages the evidence up front, so validators validate instead of reconstructing.

bands.name: GATE, SERVE, MONITOR

detail.head: Two gates before serving, one loop after it — and every No branch is a real outcome.
how: A technical gate and a model-risk gate, both with a No branch that is a real outcome
A monitoring question whose Yes re-enters the governance spine
detail.dh: Gates in the pipeline beat gates in a meeting.
detail.dec: A failed gate is a failed build with a named next step. The monitoring question’s Yes re-enters the governance spine; there is no fast path.
detail.say: Both gates have a No branch, and the No branch is exercised.

iv.short: After the registry there are two gates and one loop. The technical gate checks PR-AUC, recall at a fixed false-positive rate and p99 latency; the model-risk gate is SR 11-7 validation with SHAP reason codes and MRM approval. Then shadow, canary, champion/challenger, real-time scoring and monitoring — and a drift breach re-enters the gates. Every No branch is a real outcome.

qa.q: What does “gates in the pipeline” mean in practice?
qa.a: A failed gate is a failed build with a named next step — fix the data, or remediate and resubmit to model risk — not a debate in a meeting.

qa.q: What happens when drift is detected?
qa.a: It re-enters the governance spine. Drift triggers a governed retrain through every gate, not an automatic redeploy; there’s no fast path.
Revert the endpoint variant, or fall back to rules only. It’s instant, because the previous version is still live.

push.q: Why not auto-redeploy on drift? It’s faster.
push.a: It was explicitly rejected. A model that reaches production without validation is an unapproved model, regardless of how it got there.

nodes.name: Transaction + Customer Data
nodes.sub:
Card auth events (MSK / Kinesis)
S3 lake · RDS · device + merchant

detail.head: The authorization stream plus the slower customer, device and merchant context.
detail.role: Where the data originates, and the first place the three workloads diverge.
how: Fraud: an authorization stream measured in milliseconds
Credit: application data plus bureau files, where the file vintage itself has to be reproducible years later
AML: payment flows plus a pinned sanctions watchlist version
detail.dh: Streaming the auth events beat batch loading them.
detail.dec: Fraud is scored inside the authorization window, so the features have to be computed from a stream. Everything slower — device, merchant, customer — joins from the lake.
detail.say: Same governance spine, three completely different data shapes.

iv.short: The fraud source is the card authorization stream on MSK and Kinesis, plus slower customer, device and merchant context from the S3 lake and RDS. Fraud is scored inside the authorization window, so features have to come from the stream; everything slower joins from the lake.

qa.q: Why stream the auth events instead of batch-loading them?
qa.a: Because scoring happens inside the authorization window. Velocity features computed in a nightly batch would be hours stale for exactly the attacks they’re meant to catch.

qa.q: How do the three workloads differ at the source?
qa.a: Fraud is an authorization stream measured in milliseconds. Credit is application data plus bureau files whose vintage has to be reproducible years later. AML is payment flows plus a pinned watchlist version. Same governance spine, three completely different data shapes.

nodes.name: Ingest + Validate
nodes.sub:
PII tokenization, KMS,
lineage + governance checks

detail.head: Tokenize PII, encrypt, and attach lineage before anything is stored.
how: KMS-backed tokenisation so raw PANs never reach a feature
Schema and governance checks fail the batch, not the model
detail.dh: Governance checks on the data beat governance checks on the model.
detail.say: Governance checks run on the data before a model ever sees it.

iv.short: Ingest tokenizes PII with KMS-backed keys, encrypts, and attaches lineage before anything is stored, so a raw card number never reaches a feature. Schema and governance checks fail the batch, not the model.

qa.a: So raw PANs never reach a feature or a training set. Everything downstream works on tokens.

qa.q: What happens when a check fails?
qa.a: The batch fails. Governance checks run on the data before a model ever sees it, so a bad batch is stopped at the door instead of discovered in model behavior.

push.q: Doesn’t failing the batch delay scoring?
push.a: It delays training data, not live scoring — scoring reads the online store. A delayed batch is visible and fixable; a bad batch inside a training set isn’t.

nodes.name: Stream Feature Compute
nodes.sub:
Flink / Kinesis Analytics
velocity, entity, device counters

detail.head: Velocity and entity counters computed on the stream, inside the authorization window.
how: Flink on Kinesis Analytics for the sub-second counters
The same definitions feed the offline store for training
detail.dh: Stream compute beat recomputing features at scoring time.
detail.say: Velocity features are computed once, on the stream, and written to both stores.

iv.short: Stream feature compute runs Flink on Kinesis Analytics to produce velocity, entity and device counters inside the authorization window. The same definitions feed the offline store for training, so velocity features are computed once, on the stream, and written to both stores.

qa.q: Why compute on the stream instead of at scoring time?
qa.a: Recomputing at scoring time adds latency inside the authorization window and a second implementation that can drift from training. Computing once on the stream gives one definition for both.
Velocity counters — how often a card, device or merchant shows up in a time window — plus entity and device counters.

nodes.name: Feature Store
nodes.sub:
Online: DynamoDB p99 < 10 ms
Offline: S3 + Glue — one definition

detail.head: One feature definition serving both training and inference.
how: Offline store for training, online store for serving, from the same definition
Point-in-time correctness so a training row only sees what was knowable then
detail.dh: A managed feature store beat the hand-rolled DynamoDB plus Glue arrangement.
detail.dec: Before SageMaker Feature Store existed this was a hand-rolled DynamoDB plus Glue arrangement. The migration was worth it for the parity guarantee, not for the convenience.
detail.hard: Training-serving skew was the most expensive class of bug on the platform. A feature computed one way in a notebook and another way in the serving path changes model behavior in production with no code change anywhere.
detail.say: The feature store exists to kill training-serving skew. Everything else it does is secondary.

iv.short: The feature store serves one feature definition to both training and inference: DynamoDB online at p99 under 10 milliseconds, S3 and Glue offline. It exists to kill training-serving skew, with point-in-time correctness so a training row only sees what was knowable then.

qa.q: What is training-serving skew and why does it matter?
qa.a: A feature computed one way in a notebook and another way in serving changes model behavior in production with no code change anywhere. It was the most expensive class of bug on the platform.
Before SageMaker Feature Store existed, it was a hand-rolled DynamoDB plus Glue arrangement. The migration was worth it for the parity guarantee, not the convenience.

qa.q: What latency does the online store hit?
qa.a: p99 under 10 milliseconds on DynamoDB, which leaves room inside the 100-millisecond scoring budget.

push.q: How would you prove there’s no skew?
push.a: Both stores are written from the same definition and the online lookup sits on the same code path as training. On top of that, I’d compare the feature values logged with each decision against the offline values for the same transactions.

nodes.name: Label Store
nodes.sub:
Chargeback / dispute outcomes
confirmed 30–90 days later

detail.head: Fraud labels arrive late — a chargeback lands 30 to 90 days after the transaction.
how: Labels joined back to the originating transaction
The lag is why training sets are time-based, never random
detail.dh: Time-based splits beat random splits.
detail.hard: A random train/test split on fraud data leaks the future. The label lag forces a time-based split.
detail.say: Fraud labels are 30 to 90 days late, and the whole training design follows from that.

iv.short: Fraud labels arrive late: a chargeback or dispute lands 30 to 90 days after the transaction. The label store joins those outcomes back to the originating transaction, and that lag is why training sets are split by time, never at random.

qa.a: A random train/test split on fraud data leaks the future. The label lag forces a time-based split.

detail.hard: AML is the clearest case on the platform where the ML is easy and the governance is the entire job.
detail.say: Each workload has one gate that exists purely because of its regulator.

iv.short: The technical gate checks three things: PR-AUC, recall at a fixed false-positive rate, and p99 latency. All three pass or there’s no promotion. Recall at a fixed FPR is the headline, because the cost of a false decline is a customer-experience number we weigh explicitly.

qa.a: With fraud this rare, accuracy is meaningless — a model that approves everything looks excellent. PR-AUC and recall at a fixed false-positive rate measure what matters: catching fraud without declining good customers.

qa.q: Why is latency part of a model gate?
qa.a: Scoring happens inside the authorization window, with a p99 budget under 100 milliseconds. A more accurate model that misses the window is a worse model.
Fail fast: notify and fix the data. A technical gate failure is almost always a data problem first — a feature drifted or a label lagged.

push.q: How do you pick the false-positive rate?
push.a: It’s a business decision: the false-decline rate the bank will accept for customer experience. The gate holds recall at that fixed rate, so models are compared on the same terms.

detail.say: We didn’t make validation faster by validating less. We made the evidence arrive complete.

The pipeline packages the evidence, so validators validate instead of reconstructing.

qa.a: Not by validating less. The review queue was the real bottleneck, and bottlenecks breed shortcuts, so the pipeline packages the evidence up front — it arrives complete.

push.a: Remediate and resubmit — a formal resubmission, not negotiating the finding. MRM says no more often than people expect, and that’s the control working.

detail.dh: Progressive release beat a cutover.
detail.say: Nothing goes from validated to 100% in one step.

Nothing goes from validated to 100% in one step, and the champion/challenger evidence is what MRM sees at the next review.

qa.q: What does shadow mode tell you?
qa.a: How the new model scores real production traffic, with no customer impact, before any decision depends on it.

detail.dh: The same code path for online features beat a serving-side reimplementation.
detail.hard: For AML the hard rule is that a model may rank an alert but may never close one. Ranking improves analyst throughput; auto-closing would be unmonitored dismissal of suspicious activity.
detail.say: The model ranks the queue. A human still closes every alert.

qa.q: How do you stay under 100 ms?
qa.a: Features are precomputed on the stream and read from DynamoDB at p99 under 10 milliseconds, so the endpoint isn’t computing them at request time.

qa.q: Why the same code path as training?
qa.a: A serving-side reimplementation is exactly how training-serving skew happens.

push.q: What if the endpoint is unavailable?
push.a: Rules-only is the fallback — the same path used for rollback — so authorization never waits on the model.

detail.say: The data plane is where point-in-time correctness is won or lost.

detail.say: One governance spine serving three very different model shapes.

qa.q: Why one path for three very different models?
qa.a: It let model risk validate the pipeline once and trust every model that comes through it. Fraud, credit and AML have very different shapes, but the promotion path, the lineage and the gates are the same.

qa.q: What did governance look like before?
qa.a: Models lived on laptops with governance by spreadsheet, and validators were reconstructing models instead of validating them. Getting models off laptops was the whole first phase.

qa.q: How do you prove a model is reproducible?
qa.a: Lineage is captured at train time — data version, code and params — and training data is immutable and versioned. The POC gate was rebuilding a model from its record alone, and model risk accepted it.
100% of deployments carry lineage: every endpoint traces to its data version, code commit, params and the validation record that cleared it.

push.q: Doesn’t one path slow every team down to the speed of review?
push.a: The review queue was the real bottleneck, and bottlenecks breed shortcuts. We didn’t validate less — the pipeline packages the evidence up front, so validators validate instead of reconstructing.

qa.a: Every declined applicant gets an adverse-action notice with reasons. 100% coverage, not most — the notice is a legal artifact.

Model risk under SR 11-7, and fair lending independently, reviewing for disparate impact under Reg B.

push.a: Credit decisioning barely depends on latency, and reproducibility matters enormously. Batch Transform runs monthly for the book and on demand at origination.

dev / holdout / out-of-time

detail.dh: Out-of-time validation beat in-time holdout.
detail.dec: In-time holdout flatters every credit model because the economy has not changed. Out-of-time is the sample the validator trusts.
detail.say: Out-of-time is the sample that matters. In-time holdout flatters every credit model.

iv.short: The development sample is split into dev, holdout and out-of-time, each with a snapshot hash. Out-of-time is the sample that matters — in-time holdout flatters every credit model because the economy hasn’t changed.

qa.a: It’s the closest thing to the future the model will face. In-time holdout shares the economic conditions of training, so it flatters every model.
It pins exactly which data each sample came from, so a validator can reproduce it.

nodes.name: Segmentation + WOE Binning
nodes.sub:
Monotonic constraint design,
reason-code map defined here

detail.head: Where reason codes are designed in, not bolted on.
how: Weight-of-evidence binning with monotonic constraints
The reason-code map is a property of the binning, so adverse-action notices fall out of the model structure
detail.dh: Monotonic WOE binning beat post-hoc explanation.
detail.hard: A post-hoc explanation on an unconstrained model is not a Reg B reason code. The constraint has to be in the structure.
detail.say: Reason codes are designed at binning time, because the adverse action notice is a legal artifact.

iv.short: Segmentation and weight-of-evidence binning with monotonic constraints is where reason codes are designed in, not bolted on. The reason-code map is a property of the binning, so adverse-action notices fall out of the model structure.

qa.q: Why not explain the model afterwards with SHAP?
qa.a: A post-hoc explanation on an unconstrained model is not a Reg B reason code. The constraint has to be in the structure.
Risk only moves one way across a variable’s bins, so the reason a score went down is always coherent and explainable to the applicant.

push.q: Doesn’t the constraint cost accuracy?
push.a: Sometimes a little — that’s the trade. The XGB challenger is monotonically constrained too: if it can’t explain a decline, it can’t win.

detail.head: Where the work starts — and where it used to stop.
how: Notebooks become production scripts before anything else happens
The POC finding: models on laptops with governance-by-spreadsheet cannot be validated
detail.dh: Production scripts beat notebooks in production.
detail.dec: The POC finding was that models on laptops with governance-by-spreadsheet cannot be validated. Converting notebooks to scripts before anything else was the first control.
detail.say: Getting models off laptops was the whole first phase.

iv.short: This is where the work starts — and where it used to stop. Models lived on laptops with governance by spreadsheet, and the POC finding was that they couldn’t be validated that way. So the first control was turning notebooks into versioned production scripts before anything else happens.

qa.a: Nothing, for exploration. In production they meant models validators couldn’t reproduce — reproduction was archaeology, and sometimes impossible.
Their notebooks become versioned production scripts, built by Jenkins and trained as a pinned SageMaker job, with params and metrics logged automatically rather than by convention.

push.q: Didn’t the modellers push back?
push.a: The argument that worked was time: validators had been reconstructing models instead of validating them, and the review queue was the bottleneck. Scripts plus lineage made approvals faster, not slower.

Build / test / version
IAM · VPC · KMS · SageMaker

Change to infrastructure is a reviewed change

detail.dec: If the environment cannot be rebuilt from code, it cannot be evidence. Terraform made environment parity a control, not a convenience.
detail.say: If the environment can’t be rebuilt from code, it can’t be evidence.

iv.short: Jenkins builds, tests and versions every model artifact, and Terraform manages the infrastructure beside it — IAM, VPC, KMS and SageMaker. If an environment can’t be rebuilt from code, it can’t be evidence, so environment parity is a control, not a convenience.

qa.q: Why does infrastructure as code matter for model risk?
qa.a: Validators need to know the model ran in the environment that was tested. Terraform makes every environment rebuildable from code, and a change to infrastructure is a reviewed change.
IAM, VPC, KMS and SageMaker — the infrastructure the models train and serve in.

detail.head: One image, built once, referenced by digest everywhere.
how: The digest, not a tag, is promoted through every environment
Nothing is rebuilt for UAT or production
detail.dh: Digest promotion beat rebuilding per environment.
detail.say: Production runs the exact bytes that passed the gates.

iv.short: Amazon ECR holds one image, built once and referenced by digest everywhere. The digest — not a tag — is promoted through every environment, and nothing is rebuilt for UAT or production. Production runs the exact bytes that passed the gates.

qa.q: Why a digest instead of a tag?
qa.a: A tag can be moved to point at different bytes; a digest can’t. Promoting the digest means what was validated is exactly what runs.
A rebuild means production runs an artifact nobody tested.

Promotes the same digest
dev -> UAT -> production

qa.a: The glue between Step Functions and Jenkins drifted and broke silently. Consolidating onto one orchestrator removed a whole class of invisible failure.
Because it’s true: the migration was late in the engagement, and I’d rather date it accurately than claim it from day one.

push.q: So what did you run before?
push.a: Step Functions and Jenkins with an MLflow registry. It worked, but the glue between them was where silent failures lived.

nodes.name: SageMaker Training
nodes.sub:
PD scorecard (logistic + WOE)
monotonic XGB challenger · LGD/EAD

detail.head: A PD scorecard with a monotonic XGB challenger, plus LGD and EAD.
detail.role: Model training as a reproducible job rather than a notebook run.
how: Pinned container, pinned dependencies, pinned data version
Params and metrics logged automatically, not by convention
detail.dh: A scorecard champion with a constrained challenger beat an unconstrained model.
detail.dec: Logistic plus WOE stays explainable by construction. The XGB challenger is monotonically constrained so its reason codes remain legitimate — if it cannot explain a decline, it cannot win.
detail.hard: Without this, reproduction was archaeology — and sometimes simply impossible. That is the finding that unlocked the whole programme.
detail.say: Getting models off laptops was the whole POC. Everything after that was making it governed.

iv.short: Credit training produces a PD scorecard — logistic regression on WOE bins — as the champion, a monotonically constrained XGBoost challenger, and LGD and EAD models, all as pinned, reproducible SageMaker jobs.

qa.q: Why keep a logistic scorecard as champion?
qa.a: It’s explainable by construction. The XGB challenger is constrained so its reason codes stay legitimate — if it can’t explain a decline, it can’t win.
Loss given default and exposure at default. Together with PD they make up expected loss, which is what flows downstream into reserving.

nodes.name: Model Registry (MLflow)
nodes.sub:
Code · image digest · data hash
cut-off policy · approval state

detail.head: The one place a model version can be promoted from — with lineage and approval state attached.
how: Every registered version carries its lineage and its validation status
Nothing reaches an endpoint without a registry entry
detail.dh: A registry nothing routes around beat a spreadsheet of models.
detail.dec: If it is not in the registry, it cannot be deployed. Every entry carries code commit, image digest, data hash and approval state, so a validator reads the record instead of reconstructing it.
detail.say: If it isn’t in the registry, it can’t be deployed. That constraint is the whole design.

iv.short: MLflow is the one place a model version can be promoted from. Every entry carries the code commit, image digest, data hash, the cut-off policy and approval state, so a validator reads the record instead of reconstructing it. If it isn’t in the registry, it can’t be deployed — that constraint is the whole design.

qa.q: How do you stop people routing around the registry?
qa.a: Nothing reaches an endpoint without a registry entry, and promotion only happens from there. That’s what makes 100% of deployments traceable.

qa.q: Why version the cut-off policy with the model?
qa.a: A decision is the model plus the cut-off. Versioning them together means a decline from years ago can be reproduced exactly.
MLflow tracking was in place from the POC for runs and artifacts, so its registry became the single source of truth with lineage on every registered model.

detail.head: KS, Gini, PSI — and every declined applicant must have a reason code. 100%, not most.
detail.role: The workload-specific gate — the place where the domain regulation, not the ML, sets the bar.
how: Fraud: the cost of a false decline is a customer-experience number, and it is weighed explicitly
Credit: reason codes have to fall out of the model structure, because an adverse action notice is a legal artifact
AML: above-the-line and below-the-line testing proves the alerting threshold isn’t hiding activity underneath it
detail.dh: Reason-code coverage as a hard gate beat treating it as a report.
detail.hard: AML is the clearest case on the platform where the ML is easy and the governance is the entire job.
detail.say: Each workload has one gate that exists purely because of its regulator.

iv.short: The discriminatory-power gate: KS, Gini and PSI — and every declined applicant must have a reason code. 100%, not most. Reason-code coverage is a hard gate, not a report.

qa.q: What do KS and Gini tell you?
qa.a: How well the score separates goods from bads. PSI checks that the population hasn’t shifted away from development.
Every decline gets an adverse-action notice, and a decline without a reason code can’t be explained to the applicant.
Redevelop or rebin the sample. The fix is usually in the sample or the bins, not the estimator.

detail.head: SR 11-7 validation plus fair-lending review for disparate impact under Reg B.
detail.role: A second line of defence that does not report to the people who built the model.
how: Reviews conceptual soundness, data, testing and monitoring plan
Evidence is packaged by the pipeline so validators validate instead of reconstructing
detail.dh: A separate fair-lending reviewer beat folding it into model risk.
detail.hard: The review queue was the real bottleneck, and bottlenecks breed shortcuts. Automating evidence packaging shortened the queue without weakening the control.
detail.say: We didn’t make validation faster by validating less. We made the evidence arrive complete.

iv.short: Model risk plus fair lending: SR 11-7 validation and a separate fair-lending review for disparate impact under Reg B. Fair lending has its own independent veto, and the pipeline packages the evidence so validators validate instead of reconstructing.

qa.a: Disparate impact is its own legal question under Reg B. A separate reviewer with an independent veto beat folding it into model risk.

qa.q: How did you shorten the review queue?
qa.a: By making the evidence arrive complete. The pipeline packages it, so reviewers validate instead of reconstructing — faster without weakening the control.

nodes.name: Batch Scoring
nodes.sub:
SageMaker Batch Transform
monthly + at origination

detail.head: Batch scoring — monthly for the book, on demand at origination.
detail.role: The only route to production, and it only accepts registered, validated versions.
how: Fraud: real-time scoring inside the authorization window
Credit: decisioning where latency barely matters and reproducibility matters enormously
AML: pre-transaction sanctions screening plus ranking of rules-generated alerts
detail.dh: Batch transform beat a real-time endpoint for a decision that does not need one.
detail.hard: For AML the hard rule is that a model may rank an alert but may never close one. Ranking improves analyst throughput; auto-closing would be unmonitored dismissal of suspicious activity.
detail.say: The model ranks the queue. A human still closes every alert.

iv.short: Credit scoring is SageMaker Batch Transform — monthly for the whole book, and on demand at origination. A real-time endpoint isn’t needed for a decision where latency barely matters and reproducibility matters enormously.

qa.a: Because nothing about a credit decision needs millisecond latency, and a batch job is simpler to reproduce exactly.
Scoring the existing book, which also feeds downstream use in stress testing and reserving.

nodes.name: Decision + Adverse Action
nodes.sub:
Cut-offs, line assignment,
Reg B notice within 30 days

detail.head: Cut-offs and line assignment, with the Reg B adverse-action notice inside 30 days.
how: Every decline carries its reason codes
Cut-off policy is versioned in the registry alongside the model
detail.dh: Versioning the cut-off policy with the model beat keeping it in a config.
detail.say: The notice deadline is 30 days and the reason codes have to be right the first time.

iv.short: The decision applies cut-offs and line assignment, and every decline carries reason codes for the Reg B adverse-action notice, due within 30 days. The cut-off policy is versioned in the registry alongside the model.

qa.q: Why version the cut-off with the model?
qa.a: The decision depends on both. Keeping the cut-off in a config file means a past decision can’t be reproduced reliably.
Reg B requires the adverse-action notice within 30 days, and the reason codes have to be right the first time.

nodes.name: Score History + Audit
nodes.sub:
Every score with model and
policy version · Splunk log

detail.head: Every score retained with model and policy version, so a decision from years ago can be reproduced.
detail.role: Every decision recorded with the exact inputs and the exact model version that produced it.
how: Score history retained so a decision can be reproduced years later
Includes the feature values as served, not as recomputed
detail.dh: Retaining the inputs as served beat recomputing them.
detail.say: Reproducing a decision means reproducing the inputs too, not just the model.

iv.short: Every score is retained in a Splunk log with its model and policy version — and the inputs as served, not as recomputed — so a decision from years ago can be reproduced.

qa.q: Why keep the inputs as served?
qa.a: Recomputing them later uses today’s data and code. Reproducing a decision means reproducing the inputs too, not just the model.

detail.head: Degradation, or the annual revalidation clock — either re-enters the Model Risk Gate.
detail.role: Time-based review independent of any drift signal.
how: Driven by the model inventory, not by a detector
Credit risk in particular runs on an annual revalidation clock
detail.dh: A calendar-driven review beat relying on a detector.
detail.dec: An auto-redeploy on drift is faster and was explicitly rejected. A model that reaches production without validation is an unapproved model, regardless of how it got there.
detail.say: Some reviews are calendar-driven. A quiet model still has to be re-examined.

iv.short: Credit re-enters the model-risk gate on degradation or on the annual revalidation clock. The clock is driven by the model inventory, not by a detector — a quiet model still has to be re-examined.

qa.a: Detectors only catch what they’re built to see. A calendar review re-examines the model even when nothing has alarmed.
Credit models feed the bank’s capital numbers through CCAR, DFAST and CECL.

detail.head: The discriminatory-power gate’s No branch: redevelop or rebin the sample.
detail.dh: Going back to binning beat retuning the model.
detail.dec: If reason-code coverage or KS fails, the fix is usually in the sample or the bins, not in the estimator.
detail.say: A failed technical gate is a data problem first.

iv.short: The discriminatory-power gate’s No branch: redevelop or rebin the sample. If reason-code coverage or KS fails, the fix is usually in the sample or the bins, not in the estimator.

qa.q: Why go back to binning instead of retuning?
qa.a: Coverage and separation problems usually come from the sample or the bins. Retuning the estimator around them hides the cause.

detail.head: The model-risk gate’s No branch: remediate and resubmit.
detail.dh: A formal resubmission beat negotiating the finding.
detail.dec: MRM says no more often than people expect, and that is the control working. The finding is addressed, evidence repackaged, and the model re-enters the gate.
detail.say: MRM says no more often than people expect, and that is the control working.

iv.short: The model-risk gate’s No branch: remediate and resubmit. The finding is addressed, the evidence is repackaged, and the model re-enters the same gate. MRM says no more often than people expect, and that’s the control working.

qa.a: No — a formal resubmission beats negotiating. The model developers own the fix, and the model goes back through the same gate.

detail.head: Where the scores go next: CCAR / DFAST stress testing and CECL reserving.
detail.dh: Treating downstream capital use as a consumer beat treating it as someone else’s problem.
detail.say: A credit model is also an input to the bank’s capital numbers, which is why the revalidation clock is annual.

iv.short: Scores also flow downstream into CCAR and DFAST stress testing and CECL reserving. A credit model is an input to the bank’s capital numbers, which is why the revalidation clock is annual.

qa.q: Why does downstream use matter to the model team?
qa.a: Because a change to the model changes regulatory capital and reserve numbers, not just decisions — so change control and revalidation are stricter.

detail.head: The steady state.
detail.dh: Continuing to serve is a decision, not a default.
detail.dec: Most weeks the answer is no and the model keeps serving — but it is a recorded outcome of the monitoring question, not the absence of one.
detail.say: Most weeks the answer is no, and the model keeps serving.

iv.short: Most weeks the answer to the monitoring question is no, and the model keeps serving. But continuing is a recorded outcome of the monitoring question, not the absence of one.

qa.a: Because the question an auditor asks is whether the model was monitored, not only whether it failed. A recorded “no drift, continue” is evidence that it was.

detail.head: The bank-wide register that makes SR 11-7 enforceable, with the revalidation clock.
how: Owner, tier, validation status and revalidation date per model
detail.dh: An inventory-driven clock beat ad-hoc revalidation.
detail.say: You cannot govern models you cannot enumerate.

iv.short: The model inventory is the bank-wide register that makes SR 11-7 enforceable: owner, tier, validation status and revalidation date for every model. You can’t govern models you can’t enumerate.

qa.a: The revalidation clock — annual for credit — independent of any drift signal.
SR 11-7 applies to every model. Without a complete register, there’s no way to know which ones are overdue.

Yes — recalibrate, then re-enter the Model Risk Gate

sheet.sub: Citibank · AWS · BSA/AML and OFAC obligations · SR 11-7 validation plus above-the-line / below-the-line testing

bands.name: DATA PLANE · ENTITIES, TYPOLOGIES, LABELS

detail.head: Where payment flows and watchlists become resolved entities, typology features and a one-in-a-thousand label.
detail.role: Where the data comes from and how it becomes labels and a training set.
how: Transaction feeds and the daily-versioned watchlist arrive
Normalize + Entity Resolution builds the canonical schema and counterparty graph
AML Feature Layer computes peer baselines and typology features
Label Store joins dispositions and SAR outcomes to transactions
Curated Alert Sample builds the training set at the true base rate
Rule Set + Thresholds is pinned with model and list version
detail.dh: Entity resolution before features beat features on raw records.
detail.dec: Structuring and layering are graph patterns. You cannot see them without resolving the parties first.
detail.say: The data plane is where point-in-time correctness is won or lost.

iv.short: The AML data plane turns payment flows and watchlists into resolved entities, typology features and a one-in-a-thousand label. Wires, SWIFT, ACH, card and cash land in one canonical schema; OFAC and PEP lists are versioned daily; entity resolution builds the counterparty graph; and the label is an investigator disposition or a SAR outcome.

qa.q: Why resolve entities before computing features?
qa.a: Structuring and layering are graph patterns. You can’t see them without resolving the parties first.
About one productive alert in a thousand. Every metric has to keep that visible.
The rule set, the model and the watchlist version, as one unit.

push.q: Why not a generic anomaly detector?
push.a: Typology features beat generic anomaly scores. The bank is obliged to detect specific typologies, and coverage is checked typology by typology.

bands.name: BUILD AND PROMOTION · THE GOVERNANCE SPINE

detail.head: The governance spine — the same six stages on every Citibank workload.
how: Notebooks become production scripts, built and versioned by Jenkins with Terraform IaC
One immutable image digest promoted dev → UAT → production
Train, evaluate, package, register — nothing reaches an endpoint outside this path
detail.dh: One governed path to production beat per-team pipelines.
detail.dec: Three very different model shapes share one promotion path. That is what let model risk validate the pipeline once and trust every model that comes through it.
detail.say: One governance spine serving three very different model shapes.

iv.short: Every Citibank workload — fraud, credit and AML — goes through the same governance spine. Notebooks become production scripts, Jenkins builds and versions them with Terraform for the infrastructure, one immutable image digest is promoted from dev to UAT to production, and SageMaker trains, evaluates, packages and registers into MLflow. Nothing reaches an endpoint outside this path.

qa.q: Why one path for three very different models?
qa.a: It let model risk validate the pipeline once and trust every model that comes through it. Fraud, credit and AML have very different shapes, but the promotion path, the lineage and the gates are the same.

qa.q: What did governance look like before?
qa.a: Models lived on laptops with governance by spreadsheet, and validators were reconstructing models instead of validating them. Getting models off laptops was the whole first phase.

qa.q: How do you prove a model is reproducible?
qa.a: Lineage is captured at train time — data version, code and params — and training data is immutable and versioned. The POC gate was rebuilding a model from its record alone, and model risk accepted it.
100% of deployments carry lineage: every endpoint traces to its data version, code commit, params and the validation record that cleared it.

push.q: Doesn’t one path slow every team down to the speed of review?
push.a: The review queue was the real bottleneck, and bottlenecks breed shortcuts. We didn’t validate less — the pipeline packages the evidence up front, so validators validate instead of reconstructing.

bands.name: GATE, SERVE, MONITOR

detail.head: Two gates before serving, one loop after it — and every No branch is a real outcome.
how: A technical gate and a model-risk gate, both with a No branch that is a real outcome
A monitoring question whose Yes re-enters the governance spine
detail.dh: Gates in the pipeline beat gates in a meeting.
detail.dec: A failed gate is a failed build with a named next step. The monitoring question’s Yes re-enters the governance spine; there is no fast path.
detail.say: Both gates have a No branch, and the No branch is exercised.

iv.short: For AML, the detection gate checks precision and recall on SAR labels and typology coverage; the compliance gate is above-the-line and below-the-line testing, SR 11-7 validation and the BSA officer’s sign-off. Then two lanes — pre-transaction OFAC screening and nightly rules-engine alerts — with the model ranking the investigator queue, and typology drift re-entering ATL/BTL testing.

qa.q: What does the model actually decide?
qa.a: It ranks alerts. It never closes one — auto-closing would be unmonitored dismissal of suspicious activity. A human still closes every alert.
Sampling alerts above and below the threshold to prove the alerting threshold isn’t hiding activity underneath it. The BSA officer signs that evidence package.
Typology drift or a coverage gap re-enters ATL/BTL testing, rather than retuning a threshold in place.

push.q: Isn’t the ML the easy part here?
push.a: Yes. AML is the clearest case on the platform where the ML is easy and the governance is the entire job.

detail.head: Payment flows across every rail.
detail.role: Where the data originates, and the first place the three workloads diverge.
how: Fraud: an authorization stream measured in milliseconds
Credit: application data plus bureau files, where the file vintage itself has to be reproducible years later
AML: payment flows plus a pinned sanctions watchlist version
detail.dh: One canonical feed beat rail-specific pipelines.
detail.dec: Wires, SWIFT, ACH, card and cash all land in one schema so a typology can be seen across rails, which is exactly where layering hides.
detail.say: Same governance spine, three completely different data shapes.

iv.short: Transaction feeds cover every rail — wires, SWIFT, ACH, card and cash — landing in one canonical schema, so a typology can be seen across rails, which is exactly where layering hides.

qa.q: Why one canonical feed instead of per-rail pipelines?
qa.a: Layering moves money across rails. Per-rail pipelines would each see only part of the pattern.

how: The watchlist version is pinned with the model and rule set
A screening decision is reproducible only if the list version is known

detail.say: The watchlist is a versioned input, the same as the model.

iv.short: KYC and customer due diligence plus the OFAC and PEP watchlists, versioned daily. The watchlist version is pinned with the model and rule set, because a screening decision is only reproducible if the list version is known.

qa.a: It’s an input like the model. If you don’t know which list version screened a payment, you can’t reproduce or defend the decision.
The payment is held for L1 clearing. A screening hit stops money moving.

nodes.name: Normalize + Entity Resolution
nodes.sub:
Canonical schema; fuzzy party
matching; counterparty graph

how: Map every rail to one canonical transaction schema
Fuzzy-match parties across rails and lists into one entity
Build the counterparty graph that structuring and layering features read

detail.hard: Entity resolution is where most AML feature quality is decided. Two records for one party means two half-histories and a missed pattern.
detail.say: Structuring and layering are graph patterns. You cannot see them without resolving the parties first.

iv.short: Normalize and entity resolution maps every rail to one canonical schema, fuzzy-matches parties across rails and lists into one entity, and builds the counterparty graph that structuring and layering features read. This is where most AML feature quality is decided.

qa.q: Why does entity resolution matter so much?
qa.a: Two records for one party means two half-histories and a missed pattern.
Names and identifiers differ across rails and lists — spellings, transliterations, missing fields — so exact matching would split one party into several.

nodes.name: AML Feature Layer
nodes.sub:
Peer baselines · structuring,
layering · graph degree, community

how: Offline store for training, online store for serving, from the same definition
Point-in-time correctness so a training row only sees what was knowable then

detail.dec: Before SageMaker Feature Store existed this was a hand-rolled DynamoDB plus Glue arrangement. The migration was worth it for the parity guarantee, not for the convenience.
detail.hard: Training-serving skew was the most expensive class of bug on the platform. A feature computed one way in a notebook and another way in the serving path changes model behavior in production with no code change anywhere.
detail.say: The feature store exists to kill training-serving skew. Everything else it does is secondary.

iv.short: The AML feature layer computes peer-group baselines and typology features — structuring, layering, graph degree and community. Typology features beat generic anomaly scores, because the bank has specific typologies it’s obliged to detect.

qa.a: Comparing a customer’s activity with similar customers rather than with everyone, so what’s normal for a cash-heavy business isn’t flagged as abnormal.
Layering moves money through several parties. Degree and community in the counterparty graph show it where single-account features can’t.

Chunk on structure with overlap

detail.dec: Every filter the query layer will ever need has to exist as metadata at index time. Retrofitting one means re-indexing the corpus.
detail.say: Nothing in this layer runs at query time, and everything the query layer filters on was stamped here.

detail.say: Seven steps, one budget, and refusal is a valid output.

iv.short: Query time is everything inside the latency budget: resolve the query to concepts and expand through the ancestor closure, retrieve dense and lexical against the filtered space, fuse on rank, rerank the top-k, assemble a prompt where every passage carries its source version, generate with per-claim citations, then verify every claim — or refuse.

qa.a: In the query. Access control applied after retrieval isn’t access control — if the model has seen the text, the boundary is already crossed.
