qa.a: Because the model will fill a gap fluently when retrieval was thin. Verification maps every claim to a span; if it can’t, the claim is stripped or the answer is refused.

qa.q: Which step goes wrong most often?
qa.a: Fusion. Rank is comparable across retrievers; raw score never is. Blending scores is where most hybrid systems quietly go wrong.

push.a: Retrieval misses wearing a costume. Thin retrieval presents as a generation failure.

iv.short: Embedding vectorizes chunks for dense retrieval, in batch, with the model version recorded on every chunk. Mixing embedding versions in one index is silently wrong — the version is part of the index schema whether you treat it that way or not.

qa.a: Vectors from two models aren’t comparable, and a mixed index gives no error — just quietly wrong similarity.

qa.q: How do you change embedding models?
qa.a: Re-embed as a versioned batch job, then rerun the retrieval eval before the new vectors serve traffic.

detail.head: Writes into both retrieval surfaces at once, with a refresh path.
how: Vector field plus an analyzed text field in the same document
Incremental upserts with a refresh path for changed sources
detail.dh: Monitoring freshness beat assuming the index is current.
detail.hard: A stale index is the failure mode nobody notices, because the answers stay fluent. Freshness needs its own monitor.
detail.say: Staleness doesn’t look like an error. It looks like a confident, outdated answer.

iv.short: Index write puts each chunk into both retrieval surfaces at once — a vector field and an analyzed text field in the same document — with incremental upserts and a refresh path for changed sources. Freshness gets its own monitor, because staleness doesn’t look like an error.

qa.q: Why one document with both fields?
qa.a: Dense and lexical retrieval then read the same chunk with the same metadata and filters, so their result lists fuse cleanly.
A staleness monitor on the index write path. A stale index doesn’t error — it gives confident, outdated answers.

detail.head: The request — shorter and vaguer than the corpus vocabulary, carrying the caller’s entitlements.
how: Carries the caller’s identity and entitlements, which become filters
detail.dh: Carrying identity with the query beat looking it up later.
detail.dec: Entitlements travel with the request and become filters. That is what lets retrieval enforce access rather than the UI.
detail.say: The user’s words and the corpus’s words are rarely the same words.

iv.short: The query is usually shorter and vaguer than the corpus vocabulary, and it carries the caller’s identity and entitlements, which become filters. That’s what lets retrieval enforce access instead of the UI.

qa.q: Why carry identity with the query?
qa.a: Entitlements become filters in retrieval itself, so access is enforced before any text is retrieved — not by the UI afterwards.

qa.q: How do you bridge the vocabulary gap?
qa.a: Resolve the words to concepts first, then expand through the ancestor closure, and let dense retrieval catch the paraphrase.

detail.head: Maps the query onto the vocabulary the index is stamped with.
how: Free text resolved to entity IDs
Parent concept expands to its subtree through the precomputed ancestor closure
detail.dh: A closure filter beat a graph traversal.
detail.dec: The graph-traversal version of this is more expressive and more expensive, and puts a generated query in the hot path. The closure filter gets most of the benefit deterministically.
detail.say: Expansion is a filter over precomputed ancestors, not a live traversal.

iv.short: Resolve and expand maps the query onto the vocabulary the index is stamped with: free text resolves to entity IDs, and a parent concept expands to its whole subtree through the precomputed ancestor closure. Expansion is a filter, not a live traversal.

qa.a: It’s more expressive and more expensive, and it puts a generated query in the hot path. The closure filter gets most of the benefit deterministically.

qa.q: What happens to an unknown term?
qa.a: It doesn’t resolve, and the system says so. On J&J that rule was exact match or found:false — never a nearest-neighbour guess.

detail.head: Both retrievers run against the same filtered candidate space.
how: Dense recovers paraphrase and intent; lexical holds exact identifiers and rare terms
Filters applied in the query, so entitlements are enforced before retrieval, not after
detail.dh: Filters in the query beat post-filtering.
detail.hard: Access control applied after retrieval is not access control. If the model has seen the text, the boundary is already crossed.
detail.say: Filters go in the query. Post-filtering a result set is a security bug.

iv.short: Both retrievers run against the same filtered candidate space: dense recovers paraphrase and intent, lexical holds exact identifiers and rare terms. Filters go into the query, so entitlements are enforced before retrieval, not after.

qa.a: They fail differently. Dense misses exact identifiers; lexical misses paraphrase. Together they cover each other.
Post-filtering a result set is a security bug. If the model has seen the text, the boundary is already crossed.

detail.head: Merges two ranked lists that do not share a score scale.
how: RRF merges on rank position
No per-query-type weighting to tune and re-tune
detail.dh: Rank fusion beat score blending.
detail.dec: A BM25 score and a cosine distance are not on a comparable scale. Reciprocal rank fusion merges on position and needs no per-query weighting.
detail.say: Rank is comparable across retrievers. Raw score never is.

iv.short: Fusion merges two ranked lists that don’t share a score scale. Reciprocal rank fusion merges on rank position, with no per-query-type weighting to tune and re-tune.

qa.a: A BM25 score and a cosine distance aren’t comparable. At Home Depot, weighted blending learned on one query distribution failed on the next.

qa.q: What do you tune in RRF?
qa.a: Almost nothing — the k constant. We used 60 at Home Depot.

detail.head: Reads the query and each candidate together and reorders the top-k.
how: Applied to the top candidates only, for cost reasons
This is what turns better recall into a visible improvement
detail.dh: Reranking the top-k beat reranking everything.
detail.dec: The cross-encoder is too expensive for the full list and unnecessary beyond the top-k. Recall gets the right document into the set; reranking gets it into the top three.
detail.say: Recall gets the right document into the set. Reranking gets it into the top three.

iv.short: The reranker is a cross-encoder that reads the query and each candidate together and reorders the top-k. Recall gets the right document into the set; reranking gets it into the top three.

qa.a: A cross-encoder is too expensive for the full list and unnecessary beyond the top-k.
Related-but-not-what-I-wanted results near the top. It turns better recall into a visible improvement.

detail.head: Builds the generation prompt from reranked passages, with source and version on each.
how: Passages carry their source and version identifiers into the prompt
Context budget enforced by dropping passages, never by truncating one mid-claim
detail.dh: Dropping whole passages beat truncating one.
detail.dec: Truncating a passage mid-claim is how you manufacture a hallucination. The context budget is enforced by dropping passages, never by cutting one in half.
detail.say: Truncating a passage in half is how you manufacture a hallucination.

iv.short: Prompt assembly builds the generation context from reranked passages, each carrying its source and version. The context budget is enforced by dropping whole passages, never by truncating one mid-claim — truncation is how you manufacture a hallucination.

qa.a: A half passage can drop the qualifier that made a claim true. The model then states it with confidence and a citation.

qa.q: Why carry versions into the prompt?
qa.a: So every citation in the answer resolves to a specific document version.

detail.head: The model composes an answer over the supplied context, citing per claim.
how: Instructed to cite per claim, not per answer
Instructed that "the context does not contain this" is an acceptable output
detail.dh: Per-claim citation beat per-answer citation.
detail.hard: The model will fill a gap fluently if retrieval was thin. That is a retrieval failure presenting as a generation failure.
detail.say: Most hallucinations we chased turned out to be retrieval misses wearing a costume.

iv.short: Generation composes the answer over the supplied context, citing per claim rather than per answer, and “the context does not contain this” is an allowed output. Most hallucinations we chased were retrieval misses wearing a costume.

qa.a: So verification can check each claim against a span. A per-answer citation can’t tell you which sentence is unsupported.
Usually the model filling a gap fluently when retrieval was thin — a retrieval failure presenting as a generation failure.

push.q: Can’t you just tell the model not to hallucinate?
push.a: Instructions help, but they aren’t a control. The control is verification after generation: every claim maps to a span or it’s stripped.

detail.head: The gate between a generated answer and a user.
how: Every claim mapped back to a retrieved span
Unsupported claims are stripped or the answer is refused
Refusal rate is monitored — a sudden drop usually means the gate broke, not that quality improved
detail.dh: Refusal as a first-class output beat refusal as an error path.
detail.dec: Every claim maps to a retrieved span or it is stripped. Refusal rate is monitored in both directions — a sudden drop usually means the gate broke.
detail.say: Refusal is a feature. We alert on it moving in either direction.

iv.short: Verification is the gate between a generated answer and a user: every claim is mapped back to a retrieved span, unsupported claims are stripped or the answer is refused, and refusal rate is monitored in both directions.

qa.q: Why monitor refusal in both directions?
qa.a: A rise can mean retrieval got worse; a sudden drop usually means the gate broke, not that quality improved.

qa.q: Strip or refuse — how do you decide?
qa.a: Strip a claim when the rest of the answer stands on its own evidence; refuse when what’s left wouldn’t answer the question.

detail.head: Measures whether the right evidence was found, independently of what the model did with it.
how: Context precision and recall against a labeled set
Run on every index or chunking change
detail.dh: Separating retrieval quality from generation quality beat one end-to-end score.
detail.dec: If you only measure the final answer you will tune the wrong layer. Context precision and recall run on every index or chunking change.
detail.say: Separate retrieval quality from generation quality or you will tune the wrong layer.

iv.short: Retrieval eval measures whether the right evidence was found, independently of what the model did with it: context precision and recall against a labeled set, with RAGAS, on every index or chunking change.

qa.a: If you only measure the final answer, you’ll tune the wrong layer.
On every index or chunking change.

detail.head: Measures whether the answer is supported by the context it was given.
how: Automated judging, with the judge itself validated against human labels
Regression-gated in CI
detail.dh: A validated judge beat an unvalidated one.
detail.hard: An unvalidated LLM judge is just a second opinion with no accountability. The judge needs its own eval.
detail.say: We validate the judge before we trust the judge.

iv.short: Faithfulness eval measures whether the answer is supported by the context it was given, with RAGAS and DeepEval, regression-gated in CI — and the judge itself is validated against human labels.

qa.a: An unvalidated LLM judge is a second opinion with no accountability. The judge needs its own eval.
A faithfulness threshold, fixed before the change, enforced in CI.

detail.head: Did the user get what they actually needed.
how: Scored on realistic tasks, not on isolated question-answer pairs
detail.dh: Realistic tasks beat isolated question-answer pairs.
detail.dec: Component metrics can all pass while the product still fails the user. Task success is scored on the workflows people actually run.
detail.say: Component metrics can all pass while the product still fails the user.

iv.short: Task success asks whether the user got what they actually needed, scored on realistic tasks rather than isolated question-answer pairs. Component metrics can all pass while the product still fails the user.

qa.a: People run workflows, not single questions. A system can answer each question well and still not get the user to the outcome they needed.

detail.head: What the system actually does once real users touch it.
how: Refusal rate, citation coverage, latency, retrieval hit rate
Drift in query distribution is the early warning
detail.dh: Watching the query distribution beat watching the corpus.
detail.dec: The query distribution drifts faster than the corpus does. Refusal rate, citation coverage and retrieval hit rate are the early warnings.
stack: refusal rate · citation coverage · latency · hit rate
detail.say: The query distribution drifts faster than the corpus does.

iv.short: Online telemetry is what the system actually does once real users touch it: refusal rate, citation coverage, latency and retrieval hit rate. The query distribution drifts faster than the corpus, so that’s the early warning.

qa.a: Drift in the query distribution, and movement in refusal rate, citation coverage and retrieval hit rate.

qa.q: Why watch queries rather than the corpus?
qa.a: Users change what they ask faster than the documents change.

nums: signals: refusal · citations · latency · hit rate

detail.head: The layer no automated metric replaces.
how: A sampled set reviewed by domain experts on a cadence
Findings feed back into the labeled eval sets
detail.dh: Sampled expert review beat trusting automation.
detail.dec: Automated eval scales; SME review keeps it honest. Findings feed back into the labeled sets.
detail.say: Automated eval scales. SME review is what keeps it honest.

iv.short: SME review is the layer no automated metric replaces: domain experts review a sampled set on a cadence, and their findings feed back into the labeled eval sets. Automated eval scales; SME review keeps it honest.

qa.a: They become new labeled examples, so the automated eval learns what the experts caught.

detail.head: The composite decision: a regression on any layer blocks the release.
how: A regression on any layer blocks the release
Thresholds are agreed up front, not negotiated at release time
detail.dh: Thresholds agreed up front beat thresholds negotiated at release.
detail.say: The gate is set before the change, so nobody argues the threshold on the day.

iv.short: The release gate is the composite decision: a regression on any layer blocks the release, and thresholds are agreed up front, not negotiated at release time.

qa.a: So nobody argues the threshold on the day the numbers come in.

trace.text: 1 / 5 — Index time. Documents are parsed with layout preserved and split on structure, so a claim and its citation stay together.
2 / 5 — Every filter the query layer will ever need is stamped on now: entities, ancestors, access labels. Then embed and write to both retrieval surfaces.
3 / 5 — Query time. The question resolves to concepts, expands through the ancestor closure, and both retrievers run against the filtered space.
4 / 5 — Fuse on rank, rerank the top-k with a cross-encoder, and assemble a prompt where every passage carries its source version.
5 / 5 — Generate with per-claim citation, then verify. Unsupported claims are stripped or the answer is refused outright.

bands.name: Integration — proves the build runs

detail.head: Integration — proves the build runs.
detail.role: From pull request to a signed, digest-referenced image.
how: Pull request opens the change
Static checks and unit tests in under two minutes
Contract tests against the Service Bus message shape
Build once, push to ACR by digest
Sign with Cosign, attach an SBOM
detail.dh: Prompts as code beat prompts in a console.
detail.dec: A prompt change is a code change: reviewed, linted, unit tested, contract tested, built once. There is no console where someone edits production behaviour.
detail.say: Built once, signed, promoted by digest.

iv.short: Integration proves the build runs. The change opens as a pull request — prompts, tool schemas and fixtures reviewed as code — then static checks and unit tests in under two minutes, contract tests against the Service Bus message shape, one build pushed to ACR by digest, and a Cosign signature with an SBOM attached.

qa.a: A prompt change changes production behavior. It’s reviewed, linted, tested, contract-tested and built once — there’s no console where someone edits production behavior.
If the fast layer is slow, engineers stop trusting it and route around it.

qa.q: What do the contract tests catch?
qa.a: Hand-off drift between six independently deployed services. Coordination drift was a real production problem, and this is the cheapest place to catch it.

push.q: What about the model version itself?
push.a: Model deployments are pinned per agent with auto-upgrade disabled, so a model change goes through the same controlled path as code.

bands.name: Qualification — proves the agent behaves

detail.head: Qualification — proves the agent behaves.
detail.role: Golden-set eval, the agent-specific fixture gate, grounding, latency and cost budgets, and adversarial coverage.
how: Golden-set eval on held-out Q&A
Agent-specific fixture check — closure fixtures or seriousness recall
Grounding gate: faithfulness threshold, citation integrity pass/fail
Latency and token-cost budget
Red-team suite: injection, leakage, refusal
detail.dh: Statistical gates with fixed thresholds beat hoping the golden set passes.
detail.dec: This is the unit-test layer for an agent; it just happens to be statistical. Thresholds are fixed before the change, so nobody argues them on the day.
detail.say: Each agent has one gate that only makes sense for that agent.

iv.short: Qualification proves the agent behaves: golden-set eval on held-out Q&A, an agent-specific fixture gate, a grounding gate with a faithfulness threshold and pass/fail citation integrity, a latency and token-cost budget, and a red-team suite. It’s the unit-test layer for an agent; it just happens to be statistical.

qa.a: Knowledge runs closure-table fixtures. Drug Safety is scored on seriousness-criteria recall tuned against false negatives, plus MedDRA coding and E2B(R3) structure.

qa.q: Why fix thresholds before the change?
qa.a: So nobody argues them on the day. The gate is set first; the change has to meet it.
A reasoning-effort change can quietly triple token cost. Cost per request is gated like latency.

push.q: Isn’t an LLM-judged gate flaky?
push.a: The judge is validated against human labels, thresholds are fixed in advance, and the eval datasets are versioned, validated artifacts — so every change is measured against a stable yardstick.

bands.name: Authorization — proves someone signed

detail.head: Authorization — proves someone signed.
detail.role: Change control record, validation summary, electronic signature, and cluster admission.
how: Change control record generated from the pipeline
Validation summary packages eval results against the current production version
Part 11 electronic signature by an accountable approver
Admission control verifies the signature at the cluster door
detail.dh: Pipeline-generated evidence beat hand-assembled release paperwork.
detail.dec: The change record and validation summary are build outputs linked to the digest, so the record and the artifact cannot drift apart. A named human still signs.
detail.say: Automation gets the evidence to the desk. A person still signs.

iv.short: Authorization proves someone signed. The pipeline generates the change-control record and a validation summary against the current production version, an accountable approver applies a Part 11 electronic signature, and admission control verifies the signature at the cluster door.

qa.q: Why generate the paperwork in the pipeline?
qa.a: When the record is a build output linked to the digest, the record and the artifact can’t drift apart.
A named, accountable approver. For Drug Safety, a pharmacovigilance SME is required.
Ratify verifies the Cosign signature at admission, and Gatekeeper blocks unsigned or unapproved digests.

push.q: Doesn’t a human signature slow everything down?
push.a: Automation gets the evidence to the desk; a person still signs. The slow part used to be assembling the evidence, not reading it.

bands.name: Delivery — proves it lands safely

detail.head: Delivery — proves it lands safely.
detail.role: Staging on the same digest, a risk-sized canary, exact traffic routing on the bus, production watch, and automatic rollback.
how: Deploy to staging with the same digest
Canary rollout — 5/20/50/100 for Knowledge, 2/10/50/100 with an SME pause for Drug Safety
Route canary traffic on each agent’s topic: the orchestrator stamps a track property and the canary subscription feeds the canary pods
Watch SLOs and quality signals
Demote the ring automatically on breach
detail.dh: Canary sized to the agent’s risk beat one rollout policy.
detail.dec: The riskier the agent, the smaller the first ring and the more human the promotion. Rollback is a ring demotion, exercised on a schedule.
detail.say: You cannot split bus traffic with an ingress rule.

iv.short: Delivery proves it lands safely: staging on the same digest with the real orchestrator and bus, then a canary sized to the agent’s risk — 5, 20, 50, 100 for Knowledge; 2, 10, 50, 100 with an SME pause for Drug Safety — routed by a track property onto the topic’s canary subscription, watched on SLOs and quality signals, and demoted automatically on breach.

qa.a: The riskier the agent, the smaller the first ring and the more human the promotion.

qa.q: How do you route canary traffic on a bus?
qa.a: Not with an ingress rule. The orchestrator stamps a track property, and the topic’s canary subscription feeds the canary pods.
Any gate breach in the analysis window demotes the ring automatically, and the previous digest is still live.

push.q: Have you actually exercised the rollback?
push.a: A rollback path that’s never been run isn’t a rollback path. It gets exercised on a schedule.

detail.head: Where the change enters the system — prompts, tools and fixtures reviewed as code.
how: Prompt files, tool definitions and eval fixtures are code and are reviewed as code
A prompt change is a code change and follows the same path
detail.dh: Prompts in the repo beat prompts in a console.
detail.dec: There is no console where someone edits production behaviour. A prompt change follows the same path as a code change because it is one.
detail.say: Prompts live in the repo. There is no console where someone edits production behavior.

iv.short: The pull request is where every change enters: prompt files, tool definitions and eval fixtures are code and are reviewed as code. A prompt change follows the same path as a code change, because it is one.

qa.q: Why not let people edit prompts in a console?
qa.a: Then production behavior changes with no review, no test and no record. There is no console where someone edits production behavior.
Prompts, tool schemas and eval fixtures, together, in one pull request.

nums: reviewed as code: prompts · tools · fixtures

detail.head: The fast feedback layer — under two minutes or people route around it.
how: Runs in under two minutes or people route around it
Tool schemas type-checked against the agent contract
detail.dh: A fast layer beat a thorough-but-slow one.
detail.dec: If the fast layer is slow, engineers stop trusting it. Tool schemas are type-checked against the agent contract here.
detail.say: If the fast layer is slow, engineers stop trusting it.

iv.short: Static checks and unit tests are the fast feedback layer — lint, types and unit tests in under two minutes, with tool schemas type-checked against the agent contract. If the fast layer is slow, engineers stop trusting it.

qa.a: Past that, people route around the checks. Speed is what keeps them trusted.

qa.q: What do the type checks cover?
qa.a: Tool schemas against the agent contract, so a tool change that breaks the agent fails here.

detail.head: Verifies the agent still speaks the platform’s protocol.

Catches the hand-off drift that six independently deployed services otherwise produce

detail.say: Six services deploying independently need a contract, or they will drift apart quietly.

iv.short: Contract tests verify the agent still speaks the platform’s protocol: request and response message schemas validated against what the orchestrator expects. Six services deploying independently need a contract, or they drift apart quietly.

qa.a: Coordination drift across agents was a real production problem, and contract tests are the cheapest place to catch it.
The Service Bus request and response message shapes, against the orchestrator’s expectations.

detail.head: One image is built, once, and referenced by digest from then on.
how: The digest — not a tag — is what moves through every environment
Nothing is rebuilt for staging or for production
detail.dh: Digest promotion beat rebuilding per environment.
detail.hard: Rebuilding per environment means production runs an artifact nobody tested. Digest promotion removes the entire class of problem.
detail.say: Built once, promoted by digest. Production runs the exact bytes that passed the gates.

iv.short: One image is built, once, and referenced by digest from then on. The digest — not a tag — moves through every environment, and nothing is rebuilt for staging or production. Production runs the exact bytes that passed the gates.

qa.q: How do six services share an image?

detail.head: Cryptographic provenance on the artifact.
how: Cosign signature plus an SBOM attached to the digest
Verified again at admission, inside the cluster

detail.dec: The signature is checked at the cluster door, not just at the build. An unsigned or mismatched digest cannot be scheduled.
detail.say: The signature is checked at the door, not just at the build.

qa.a: The last enforcement point should be the cluster itself. A signature checked only at build can be bypassed by anything that skips the pipeline.

detail.head: The behavioural regression suite.
how: A curated question set with document-backed answers
Scored on retrieval and faithfulness, thresholds fixed in advance
detail.dh: A curated set with fixed thresholds beat an ad-hoc smoke test.
detail.dec: A curated question set with document-backed answers, scored on retrieval and faithfulness. Thresholds are fixed in advance.
detail.say: This is the unit test layer for an agent. It just happens to be statistical.

iv.short: Golden-set eval is the behavioral regression suite: a curated, held-out question set with document-backed answers, scored on retrieval and faithfulness, with thresholds fixed in advance. It’s the unit-test layer for an agent; it just happens to be statistical.

qa.q: Where does the golden set come from?
qa.a: Curated questions with document-backed answers, held out from anything used to tune the agent. SME review findings feed new examples in.
Retrieval and faithfulness, against thresholds set before the change.

detail.head: The gate that exists because of what this specific agent is for.
how: Knowledge agent: fixtures assert that a parent-concept query returns the whole subtree — a broken closure build shows up here, not in production
Drug Safety agent: recall on seriousness criteria, deliberately tuned against false negatives, plus MedDRA coding and E2B(R3) structure checks
detail.dh: Agent-specific gates beat one generic eval.
detail.hard: For Drug Safety, overall accuracy is the wrong headline metric. A missed serious event costs more than several false flags, and the threshold reflects that asymmetry.
detail.say: Each agent has one gate that only makes sense for that agent. That’s the point of specialists.

qa.a: Each specialist exists for a reason, and its gate should test that reason. That’s the point of specialists.
Overall accuracy is the wrong headline. A missed serious event costs more than several false flags, and the threshold reflects that asymmetry.

Citation integrity is pass/fail, not a threshold to negotiate

detail.say: Faithfulness has a threshold. Citation integrity does not — it either holds or the build fails.

iv.short: The grounding gate is the hard gate on whether answers are supported: faithfulness scored by a validated judge against a threshold, and citation integrity as pass/fail. Faithfulness has a threshold; citation integrity doesn’t — it holds or the build fails.

qa.a: A citation either resolves to evidence the agent was given or it doesn’t. There’s nothing to negotiate.
A judge validated against human labels.

Token cost per request tracked, because a reasoning-effort change can quietly triple it

Linked to the digest, so the record and the artifact cannot drift apart

Eval datasets referenced by their own validated version

detail.say: The eval dataset is version-controlled and validated, the same as the code.

iv.short: The validation summary packages the eval results in the form a validation reviewer needs: thresholds, results and deltas against the current production version, with each eval dataset referenced by its own validated version.

qa.a: If the test set can change silently, the evidence means nothing. Eval datasets are controlled artifacts, the same as code.
A reviewer’s real question is whether this version is better or worse than what’s running now.

detail.head: A named, accountable human approves the release.
how: Part 11 compliant signature bound to the identity and the timestamp
For the Drug Safety agent, a pharmacovigilance SME is a required approver
detail.dh: A required SME approver for Drug Safety beat a single generic approver.
detail.dec: For the Drug Safety agent a pharmacovigilance SME is a required approver. The signature is bound to identity and timestamp under Part 11.
detail.say: Automation gets the evidence to the desk. A person still signs.

iv.short: A named, accountable human approves the release with a Part 11 electronic signature, bound to identity and timestamp. For the Drug Safety agent, a pharmacovigilance SME is a required approver. Automation gets the evidence to the desk; a person still signs.

qa.q: Why require an SME for Drug Safety?
qa.a: Because the risk is clinical, not technical. A generic approver can’t judge a change to seriousness-criteria behavior.
The signature is bound to an authenticated identity and a timestamp, and it’s linked to the digest it approves.

detail.head: The cluster refuses anything that cannot prove where it came from.
how: Ratify verifies the Cosign signature at admission
Gatekeeper policy blocks unsigned or unapproved digests
detail.dh: Enforcement at the cluster beat enforcement only in the pipeline.
detail.dec: The last enforcement point is the cluster itself. Ratify verifies the Cosign signature; Gatekeeper policy blocks unsigned or unapproved digests.
detail.say: The last enforcement point is the cluster itself, not the pipeline that fed it.

iv.short: Admission control means the cluster refuses anything that can’t prove where it came from: Ratify verifies the Cosign signature at admission, and Gatekeeper policy blocks unsigned or unapproved digests. The last enforcement point is the cluster itself.

qa.a: Pipelines can be bypassed. If the cluster checks the signature, nothing unsigned runs, however it arrived.

detail.head: Full-platform rehearsal with the real orchestrator and the real bus.
how: Same digest that will go to production
Cross-agent contract verified live, not in isolation
detail.dh: Testing the platform beat testing the container.
detail.dec: Staging runs the same digest against the real orchestrator so the cross-agent contract is verified live, not in isolation.
detail.say: Staging tests the platform, not the container.

iv.short: Staging is a full-platform rehearsal: the same digest that will go to production, running against the real orchestrator and the real bus, so the cross-agent contract is verified live, not in isolation. Staging tests the platform, not the container.

qa.q: Why test against the real orchestrator?
qa.a: Because the risk is in the hand-offs. A container can pass alone and still break the conversation with the orchestrator.

detail.head: Progressive delivery with automated analysis between steps.
how: Knowledge agent: 5, 20, 50, 100 with automated gate analysis at each step
Drug Safety agent: a slower 2, 10, 50, 100 with a mandatory pharmacovigilance SME pause before the final promotion
Rollback is a demotion of the ring, not a fresh deploy
detail.dh: Risk-sized rings beat one rollout policy.
detail.dec: Knowledge goes 5, 20, 50, 100 with automated analysis. Drug Safety goes 2, 10, 50, 100 with a mandatory SME pause before the final promotion.
detail.say: The riskier the agent, the smaller the first ring and the more human the promotion.

iv.short: The canary is progressive delivery with automated analysis between steps. Knowledge goes 5, 20, 50, 100 with automated gate analysis; Drug Safety goes a slower 2, 10, 50, 100 with a mandatory pharmacovigilance SME pause before the final promotion. Rollback is a ring demotion, not a fresh deploy.

qa.a: The riskier the agent, the smaller the first ring and the more human the promotion.
Argo Rollouts, with analysis between steps on latency, errors, subscription backlog, refusal rate and citation coverage.

detail.head: The hard part: canary on a message bus is not the same as canary behind an ingress.
how: Chosen: a topic per agent with stable and canary subscriptions; the orchestrator stamps a track property and subscription filters route each message deterministically
Rejected: two KEDA ScaledObjects and a replica ratio, which only approximates the share of messages on the new version
detail.dh: A topic per agent with stable and canary subscriptions beat a replica-ratio approximation.
detail.dec: The orchestrator stamps a track property at the rollout step’s weight, hashing the session ID so a conversation stays on one version. Subscription filters send canary-tracked messages to the canary pods. The Drug Safety 2% first ring is only exact this way; with replicas it would need about fifty pods per canary pod, and KEDA would drift the ratio with load.
detail.hard: Replica ratio is a probabilistic approximation of a traffic split. For a governed agent, "roughly five percent" is not an acceptable description of what a regulator was told.
detail.say: You can’t split bus traffic with an ingress rule. We route it explicitly: a topic per agent, a track property, and a canary subscription.

iv.short: Canary on a message bus isn’t canary behind an ingress. Each agent has a topic with stable and canary subscriptions; the orchestrator stamps a track property at the rollout step’s weight, hashing the session ID so a conversation stays on one version, and subscription filters send canary-tracked messages to the canary pods.

qa.a: Two KEDA ScaledObjects and a replica ratio. It needs no orchestrator change, but it only approximates the share of messages on the new version, and KEDA drifts the ratio with load.
For a governed agent, “roughly five percent” isn’t an acceptable description of what a regulator was told. Drug Safety’s 2% first ring is only exact this way.
A publisher change in the orchestrator and a second subscription per agent — for an exact, auditable split.

qa.q: How many pods would replicas need?
qa.a: About fifty pods per canary pod to approximate 2%.

nums: pods a replica ratio would need

push.q: Why hash the session ID?
push.a: So one conversation stays on one version. Otherwise a single session could bounce between the old and new agent mid-conversation.

detail.head: The canary analysis window, using product signals rather than just infrastructure ones.
how: Latency, error rate and subscription backlog
Refusal rate and citation coverage, which move before the infrastructure metrics do
detail.dh: Quality signals beat CPU as the canary metric.
detail.dec: For an agent, quality metrics degrade before CPU ever notices. Refusal rate and citation coverage are in the analysis alongside latency and subscription backlog.
detail.say: For an agent, quality metrics degrade before CPU ever notices.

iv.short: Production watch is the canary analysis window, using product signals rather than just infrastructure ones: latency, error rate and subscription backlog, plus refusal rate and citation coverage — which move before the infrastructure metrics do.

qa.q: Why quality signals in a canary?
qa.a: For an agent, quality degrades before CPU ever notices. Refusal rate and citation coverage catch a bad version that’s perfectly healthy as a container.
On a bus, a slow agent shows up as messages piling up on its subscription before it shows up as errors.

nums: signals: latency · errors · backlog · refusal · citations

detail.head: The failure path, exercised deliberately.
how: Any gate breach in the analysis window demotes the ring automatically
Previous digest is still live, so rollback is instant
detail.dh: A rehearsed rollback beat a theoretical one.
detail.hard: A rollback path that has never been run is not a rollback path. It gets exercised on a schedule.
detail.say: We test the rollback, not just the release.

iv.short: Automated rollback is the failure path, exercised deliberately: any gate breach in the analysis window demotes the ring automatically, and because the previous digest is still live, rollback is instant. We test the rollback, not just the release.

qa.a: A rollback path that has never been run isn’t a rollback path. It gets exercised on a schedule.
Demotion moves traffic back to the previous digest, which never stopped running.

trace.text: 1 / 5 — Integration. A prompt change is a code change: it gets reviewed, linted, unit tested, and checked against the Service Bus message contract.
2 / 5 — One image, built once, signed, and referenced by digest from here to production. Nothing is ever rebuilt downstream.
3 / 5 — Qualification. Golden-set eval, the agent-specific fixture gate, hard citation integrity, and an adversarial suite that treats retrieved content as untrusted input.
4 / 5 — Authorization. The pipeline emits the change record and validation summary, an accountable human signs under Part 11, and the cluster verifies the signature at admission.
5 / 5 — Delivery. Staging on the same digest, then a canary sized to the agent’s risk, routed by message property, watched on quality signals, with automatic demotion on breach.
